{{Short description|Health of populations in a global context}}
{{Cs1 config|name-list-style=vanc}}
{{For|the bibliographic database|Global Health database}}
{{pp-vandalism|small=yes}}
[[File:World Health Organisation building from south.jpg|thumb| The [[World Health Organization]] in [[Geneva]], [[Switzerland]]]]

'''Global health''' is the [[health]] of populations in a worldwide context;<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Brown TM, Cueto M, Fee E | title = The World Health Organization and the transition of "international" to "global" public health | journal = American Journal of Public Health | volume = 96 | issue = 1 | pages = 62–72 | date = January 2006 | pmid = 16322464 | pmc = 1470434 | doi = 10.2105/AJPH.2004.050831 }}</ref> it has been defined as "the area of study, [[research]], and practice that places a priority on improving health and achieving equity in health for all people worldwide".<ref name="Koplan">{{cite journal | vauthors = Koplan JP, Bond TC, Merson MH, Reddy KS, Rodriguez MH, Sewankambo NK, Wasserheit JN | title = Towards a common definition of global health | journal = Lancet | volume = 373 | issue = 9679 | pages = 1993–5 | date = June 2009 | pmid = 19493564 | doi = 10.1016/S0140-6736(09)60332-9 | pmc = 9905260 | bibcode = 2009Lanc..373.1993K | s2cid = 6919716 | citeseerx = 10.1.1.610.7968 }}</ref> Problems that transcend national borders or have a global political and economic impact are often emphasized.<ref>{{cite book | last = Global Health Initiative | title = Why Global Health Matters | publisher = FamiliesUSA | year = 2008 | location = Washington, DC | url = http://www.familiesusa.org/issues/global-health/matters/ | access-date = 2008-06-10 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20110308223639/http://www.familiesusa.org/issues/global-health/matters/ | archive-date = 2011-03-08 }}</ref> Thus, global health is about worldwide health improvement ([[Global mental health|including mental health]]), reduction of [[Health disparities|disparities]], and protection against [[global threats]] that disregard national borders,<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Macfarlane SB, Jacobs M, Kaaya EE | title = In the name of global health: trends in academic institutions | journal = Journal of Public Health Policy | volume = 29 | issue = 4 | pages = 383–401 | date = December 2008 | pmid = 19079297 | doi = 10.1057/jphp.2008.25 | s2cid = 46424271 }}</ref><ref name="pmid32381654">{{cite journal | vauthors = Fischer SE, Patil P, Zielinski C, Baxter L, Bonilla-Escobar FJ, Hussain S, Lai C, Walpole SC, Ohanyido F, Flood D, Singh A, Al-Shorbaji N | display-authors = 6 | title = Is it about the 'where' or the 'how'? Comment on ''Defining global health as public health somewhere else'' | journal = BMJ Global Health | volume = 5 | issue = 5 | date = May 2020 | article-number = e002567 | pmid = 32381654 | pmc = 7223010 | doi = 10.1136/bmjgh-2020-002567 }}</ref> including [[List of causes of death by rate|the most common causes of human death and years of life lost]] from a global perspective.

Global health is not to be confused with [[international health]], which is defined as the branch of [[public health]] focusing on [[Developing country|developing nations]] and [[Aid|foreign aid]] efforts by [[Developed country|industrialized countries]].<ref>{{cite book |vauthors=White F, Nanan DJ |chapter=International and Global Health | veditors = Wallace RB |title= Maxcy-Rosenau-Last Public Health and Preventive Medicine |publisher=McGraw Hill |year=2008 |isbn=978-0-07-144198-8 |pages=1252–8 |edition=15th}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|title=Comparing Approaches to Research in Global and International Health: An Exploratory Study|journal=Annals of Global Health|date=2020-04-29|issn=2214-9996|pmc=7193757|pmid=32377512|pages=47|volume=86|issue=1|doi=10.5334/aogh.2799|first1=Kristy C. Y.|last1=Yiu|first2=Eva Merethe|last2=Solum|first3=Deborah D.|last3=DiLiberto|first4=Steffen|last4=Torp |doi-access=free }}</ref>

One way that global health can be measured is through the prevalence of various global [[disease]]s in the world and their threat to decrease [[life expectancy]] in the present day. Estimates suggest that in a pre-modern, poor world, life expectancy was around 30 years in all regions of the world (mainly due to high [[infant mortality]]).<ref>{{Cite journal| vauthors = [[Max Roser|Roser M]], Ortiz-Ospina E, [[Hannah Ritchie|Ritchie H]] |date=2013-05-23|title=Life Expectancy|url=https://ourworldindata.org/life-expectancy|journal=Our World in Data}}</ref> Another<!--related and similar--> holistic perspective called [[One Health]] can<!--is sometimes used to address/invoked when addressing--> be used to address [[List of global issues|global health challenges]] and to improve global [[health security]].<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Conrad PA, Meek LA, Dumit J | title = Operationalizing a One Health approach to global health challenges | journal = Comparative Immunology, Microbiology and Infectious Diseases | volume = 36 | issue = 3 | pages = 211–6 | date = May 2013 | pmid = 23711930 | doi = 10.1016/j.cimid.2013.03.006 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Hernando-Amado S, Coque TM, Baquero F, Martínez JL | title = Defining and combating antibiotic resistance from One Health and Global Health perspectives | journal = Nature Microbiology | volume = 4 | issue = 9 | pages = 1432–42 | date = September 2019 | pmid = 31439928 | doi = 10.1038/s41564-019-0503-9 | s2cid = 201283254 | url = https://digitalcommons.fiu.edu/srhreports/health/health/43 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Sinclair JR | title = Importance of a One Health approach in advancing global health security and the Sustainable Development Goals | journal = Revue Scientifique et Technique | volume = 38 | issue = 1 | pages = 145–154 | date = May 2019 | pmid = 31564744 | doi = 10.20506/rst.38.1.2949 | s2cid = 203608381 }}</ref>

The predominant agency associated with global health (and international health) is the [[World Health Organization]] (WHO). Other important agencies impacting global health include [[UNICEF]] and [[World Food Programme]] (WFP). The [[United Nations]] system has also played a part in cross-sectoral actions to address global health and its underlying [[Social determinants of health|socioeconomic determinants]] with the declaration of the [[Millennium Development Goals]]<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.un.org/millenniumgoals/ |title=Millennium Development Goals |publisher=United Nations |access-date=2013-03-15}}</ref> and the more recent [[Sustainable Development Goals]]. The field of [[global health law]] studies international lawmaking bodies, such as the WHO, and their effect on global health.

==Definition==
[[File:Open Global Health at OpenCon 2015.jpg|thumb|Open Global Health at OpenCon 2015]]
Global health employs several perspectives that focus on the determinants and distribution of health in international contexts.

* [[Medicine]] describes the [[pathology]] of diseases and promotes [[preventive healthcare|prevention]], [[diagnosis]], and [[Medical treatment|treatment]].<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Weatherall DJ, Clegg JB | title = Inherited haemoglobin disorders: an increasing global health problem | journal = Bulletin of the World Health Organization | volume = 79 | issue = 8 | pages = 704–712 | year = 2001 | pmid = 11545326 | pmc = 2566499 }}</ref>
* [[Public health]] emphasizes the health of populations.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Fried LP, Bentley ME, Buekens P, Burke DS, Frenk JJ, Klag MJ, Spencer HC | title = Global health is public health | journal = Lancet | volume = 375 | issue = 9714 | pages = 535–7 | date = February 2010 | pmid = 20159277 | doi = 10.1016/s0140-6736(10)60203-6 | s2cid = 38796542 }}</ref>
* [[Epidemiology]] helps identify risk factors and causes of health problems.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Ahern M, Kovats RS, Wilkinson P, Few R, Matthies F | title = Global health impacts of floods: epidemiologic evidence | journal = Epidemiologic Reviews | volume = 27 | issue = 1 | pages = 36–46 | year = 2005 | pmid = 15958425 | doi = 10.1093/epirev/mxi004 | doi-access = free }}</ref>
* [[Demography]] provides data for policy decisions.<ref>{{cite book | vauthors = Verano JW, Ubelake DH |title=Disease and demography in the Americas |date=1992 |publisher=Smithsonian Institution Press |location=Washington |isbn=978-1-56098-163-3}}</ref>
* [[Economics]] emphasizes the cost-effectiveness and cost-benefit approaches for the optimal allocation of health resources.<ref>{{cite report | vauthors = Bloom DE, Cafiero E, Jané-Llopis E, Abrahams-Gessel S, Bloom LR, Fathima S, Feigl AB, Gaziano T, Hamandi A, Mowafi M, O'Farrell D | display-authors = 6 | title = The global economic burden of noncommunicable diseases. | work = Program on the Global Demography of Aging | date = January 2012 | url = https://ideas.repec.org/p/gdm/wpaper/8712.html }}</ref>
* Other social sciences such as [[sociology]], [[development studies]], [[psychology]], [[anthropology]], [[cultural studies]], and [[law]] can help understand the determinants of health in societies.

Both individuals and organizations working in the domain of global health often face many questions regarding [[ethics|ethical]] and [[human rights]]. Critical examination of the various causes and justifications of health inequities is necessary for the success of proposed solutions. Such issues are discussed at the bi-annual Global Summits of National Ethics/Bioethics Councils.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.globalsummit-berlin2016.de/ | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20190404102034/https://www.globalsummit-berlin2016.de/ | archive-date = 4 April 2019 | title = Global Summits of National Ethics/Bioethics Councils | location = Berlin | date = 2016 }}</ref>

==History==
{{see also|Timeline of global health}}
[[File:Life expectancy by world region since 1770, OWID.svg|thumb|Life expectancy by world region, from 1770 to 2018]]

Important steps were taken towards global co-operation in health with the formation of the [[United Nations]] (UN) and the [[World Bank Group]] in 1945, after [[World War II]]. In 1948, the member states of the newly formed United Nations gathered to create the [[World Health Organization]]. A cholera epidemic that took 20,000 lives in Egypt in 1947 and 1948 helped spur the international community to action.<ref>{{cite web|title=History of WHO|author=World Health Organization|url=https://www.who.int/library/historical/access/who/index.en.shtml|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061207150944/http://www.who.int/library/historical/access/who/index.en.shtml|archive-date=2006-12-07}}</ref> The WHO published its [[WHO Model List of Essential Medicines|Model List of Essential Medicines]], and the 1978 [[Alma Ata declaration]] underlined the importance of [[primary health care]].<ref>{{cite report|title=Primary Health Care: Report of the International Conference on Primary Health Care|location=Geneva|publisher=World Health Organization|year=1978|url=http://www.unicef.org/about/history/files/Alma_Ata_conference_1978_report.pdf|access-date=2014-05-06|archive-date=2017-08-29|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170829195121/https://www.unicef.org/about/history/files/Alma_Ata_conference_1978_report.pdf}}</ref>

At a United Nations Summit in 2000, member nations declared eight [[Millennium Development Goals]] (MDGs),<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Kumar S, Kumar N, Vivekadhish S | title = Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) to Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs): Addressing Unfinished Agenda and Strengthening Sustainable Development and Partnership | journal = Indian Journal of Community Medicine | volume = 41 | issue = 1 | pages = 1–4 | date = January–March 2016 | pmid = 26917865 | pmc = 4746946 | doi = 10.4103/0970-0218.170955 | doi-access = free }}</ref> which reflected the major challenges facing human development globally, to be achieved by 2015.<ref>{{cite web|title=Resolution adopted by the General Assembly, 55/2|date=18 September 2000|publisher=United Nations|url=https://www.un.org/millennium/declaration/ares552e.pdf}}</ref> The declaration was matched by unprecedented global investment by donor and recipient countries. According to the UN, these MDGs provided an important framework for development and significant progress has been made in a number of areas.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web
| url = https://sustainabledevelopment.un.org/post2015/transformingourworld
| title = Transforming our world: the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development .:. Sustainable Development Knowledge Platform
| website = sustainabledevelopment.un.org
| access-date = 2016-02-26
}}</ref>  However, progress has been uneven and some of the MDGs were not fully realized including [[Maternal health|maternal]], newborn and child health and [[reproductive health]].<ref name=":0" /> Building on the MDGs, a new Sustainable Development Agenda with 17 [[Sustainable Development Goals]] (SDGs) has been established for the years 2016–2030.<ref name=":0" />  The first goal being an ambitious and historic pledge to [[Sustainable Development Goal 1|end poverty]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web
| url = http://www.undp.org/content/undp/en/home/sdgoverview/
| title = Sustainable Development Goals
| website = UNDP
| access-date = 2016-02-26
| archive-date = 2016-03-04
| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160304031536/http://www.undp.org/content/undp/en/home/sdgoverview/
}}</ref> On 25 September 2015, the 193 countries of the UN General Assembly adopted the 2030 Development Agenda titled ''Transforming our world: the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development''.<ref name=":1" />

Several major initiatives began in the 2000s, including the vaccine alliance [[GAVI]] in 2000, [[The Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria]] in 2002, U.S. [[President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief]] in 2003, and the U.S. [[President's Malaria Initiative]] in 2005. In this decade and as part of the [[Monterrey Consensus]] (which did not pursue goals as aggressively as many activists had urged),<ref>{{cite news | vauthors = Price N |title=Countries gather to fight poverty |url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/647423631/ |access-date=21 November 2022 |work=The Sacramento Bee |date=March 23, 2002 |page=A13 }}</ref> an increasing emphasis was put on measuring improvement in health outcomes, rather than merely the amount of money spent.<ref>{{cite web | vauthors = Mark Dybul M | work = The Catalyst | publisher = George W. Bush Institute | url = https://www.bushcenter.org/catalyst/africa/dybul-advance-of-global-health.html | title = How HIV, SARS, and Ebola Put Global Health on the Agenda | date = Summer 2017 }}</ref>

In 2015 a book titled ''[[To Save Humanity]]'' was published, with nearly 100 essays regarding today's most pressing global health issues.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Hoffman SJ | title = Ending medical complicity in state-sponsored torture | journal = Lancet | volume = 378 | issue = 9802 | pages = 1535–7 | date = October 2011 | pmid = 21944647 | doi = 10.1016/S0140-6736(11)60816-7 | ssrn = 2725729 | s2cid = 45829194 }}</ref> The essays were authored by global figures in politics, science, and advocacy ranging from [[Bill Clinton]] to [[Peter Piot]], and addressed a wide range of issues including [[vaccination]]s, [[antimicrobial resistance]], [[Universal health care|health coverage]], [[Tobacco smoking|tobacco use]], research methodology, [[climate change]], equity, access to medicine, and media coverage of health research.

Global health as a discipline is frequently regarded to be of imperial origin, and there have been calls for its decolonisation.<ref>{{cite journal |display-authors=6 |vauthors=Kwete X, Tang K, Chen L, Ren R, Chen Q, Wu Z, Cai Y, Li H |date=January 2022 |title=Decolonizing global health: what should be the target of this movement and where does it lead us? |journal=Global Health Research and Policy |volume=7 |issue=1 |article-number=3 |doi=10.1186/s41256-022-00237-3 |pmc=8784247 |pmid=35067229 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Rasheed MA |date=December 2021 |title=Navigating the violent process of decolonisation in global health research: a guideline |journal=The Lancet. Global Health |volume=9 |issue=12 |pages=e1640–1 |doi=10.1016/S2214-109X(21)00440-X |pmid=34798014 |s2cid=244286291 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Affun-Adegbulu C, Adegbulu O |date=August 2020 |title=Decolonising Global (Public) Health: from Western universalism to Global pluriversalities |journal=BMJ Global Health |volume=5 |issue=8 |article-number=e002947 |doi=10.1136/bmjgh-2020-002947 |pmc=7443258 |pmid=32819916 |s2cid=221220715}}</ref> The global health ecosystem has also been criticised as having a feudal structure, acting for a small group of institutions and individuals based in high-income countries which acts similar to an imperial "Crown".<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Keshri VR, Bhaumik S |date=September 2022 |title=The feudal structure of global health and its implications for decolonisation |journal=BMJ Global Health |volume=7 |issue=9 |article-number=e010603 |doi=10.1136/bmjgh-2022-010603 |pmc=9516156 |pmid=36167407 |s2cid=252565623}}</ref>

==Measures==
Measures of global health include [[disability-adjusted life year]] (DALY), [[quality-adjusted life year]]s (QALYs), and [[mortality rate]].<ref name="etches2006">{{cite journal | vauthors = Etches V, Frank J, Di Ruggiero E, Manuel D | title = Measuring population health: a review of indicators | journal = Annual Review of Public Health | volume = 27 | pages = 29–55 | year = 2006 | pmid = 16533108 | doi = 10.1146/annurev.publhealth.27.021405.102141 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

===Disability-adjusted life years===
[[Image:All causes DALYs per 100,000 people gradient world map (2021).svg|thumb|Disability-adjusted life years per 100,000 people in 2021:<div style="text-align: left">
{{legend|#e0e0e0|no data}}
{{legend|#ffffcc|less than 23,500}}
{{legend|#ffeda0|23,500-31,000}}
{{legend|#fed976|31,000-38,500}}
{{legend|#feb24c|38,500-46,000}}
{{legend|#fd8d3c|46,000-53,500}}
{{legend|#fc4e2a|53,500-61,000}}
{{legend|#e31a1c|61,000-68,500}}
{{legend|#bd0026|68,500-76,000}}
{{legend|#800026|more than 76,000}}
</div>]]
{{Main|Disability-adjusted life year}}
The DALY is a summary measure that combines the impact of [[illness]], [[disability]], and mortality by measuring the time lived with disability and the time lost due to premature mortality. One DALY can be thought of as one lost year of "healthy" life. The DALY for a disease is the sum of the years of life lost due to premature mortality and the years lost due to disability for incident cases of the health condition.

===Quality-adjusted life years===
{{Main|Quality-adjusted life year}}
QALYs combine expected survival with expected [[Quality of life (healthcare)|quality of life]] into a single number: if an additional year of healthy life is worth a value of one (year), then a year of less healthy life is worth less than one (year). QALY calculations are based on measurements of the value that individuals place on expected years of survival. Measurements can be made in several ways: by techniques that replicate gambles about preferences for alternative states of health, with surveys or analyses that infer willingness to pay for alternative states of health, or through instruments that are based on trading off some or all likely survival time that a medical intervention might provide in order to gain less survival time of higher quality.<ref name="etches2006" />

===Infant and child mortality===
{{Main|Infant mortality|Child mortality}}
Infant mortality and child mortality for children under age 5 are more specific than DALYs or QALYs in representing the health in the poorest sections of a population, and are thus especially useful when focusing on [[health equity]].<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Mulholland E, Smith L, Carneiro I, Becher H, Lehmann D | title = Equity and child-survival strategies | journal = Bulletin of the World Health Organization | volume = 86 | issue = 5 | pages = 399–407 | date = May 2008 | pmid = 18545743 | pmc = 2647438 | doi = 10.2471/BLT.07.044545 }}</ref> added section

===Morbidity===
{{Main|Morbidity}}
Morbidity measures include [[incidence rate]], [[prevalence]], and [[cumulative incidence]], with incidence rate referring to the risk of developing a new health condition within a specified period of time. Although sometimes loosely expressed simply as the number of new cases during a time period, morbidity is better expressed as a proportion or a rate.

==Health topics==
===Infectious diseases===

==== Respiratory tract infections ====
{{Main|Respiratory tract infection}}
Infections of the respiratory tract and middle ear are major causes of morbidity and mortality worldwide.<ref name="Lopez AD 2006">{{cite journal | vauthors = Lopez AD, Mathers CD, Ezzati M, Jamison DT, Murray CJ | title = Global and regional burden of disease and risk factors, 2001: systematic analysis of population health data | journal = Lancet | volume = 367 | issue = 9524 | pages = 1747–57 | date = May 2006 | pmid = 16731270 | doi = 10.1016/S0140-6736(06)68770-9 | s2cid = 22609505 }}</ref> Some respiratory infections of global significance include [[tuberculosis]], [[measles]], [[influenza]], [[coronavirus]]es and [[pneumonia]]s caused by ''[[Mycobacterium tuberculosis]]'', ''[[Morbillivirus]]'', ''[[Haemophilus influenzae]] and [[Pneumococci]]'' respectively. The spread of respiratory infections is exacerbated by crowded conditions, and poverty is associated with more than a 20-fold increase in the relative burden of [[lung infections]].<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Mizgerd JP | title = Lung infection--a public health priority | journal = PLOS Medicine | volume = 3 | issue = 2 | article-number = e76 | date = February 2006 | pmid = 16401173 | pmc = 1326257 | doi = 10.1371/journal.pmed.0030076 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

==== Diarrheal illnesses ====
{{Main|Diarrhea}}
[[Diarrhea]] is the second most common cause of child mortality worldwide, responsible for 17% of deaths of children under age 5.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.childinfo.org/709.htm |title=Statistics by Area — Diarrhoeal disease — The challenge |publisher=UNICEF |access-date=2013-01-12}}</ref> Poor [[sanitation]] can increase transmission of bacteria and viruses through water, food, utensils, hands, and flies. Dehydration due to diarrhea can be effectively treated through [[oral rehydration therapy]] with dramatic reductions in mortality.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Taylor CE, Greenough WB | title = Control of diarrheal diseases | journal = Annual Review of Public Health | volume = 10 | pages = 221–244 | year = 1989 | pmid = 2655632 | doi = 10.1146/annurev.pu.10.050189.001253 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Victora CG, Bryce J, Fontaine O, Monasch R | title = Reducing deaths from diarrhoea through oral rehydration therapy | journal = Bulletin of the World Health Organization | volume = 78 | issue = 10 | pages = 1246–55 | year = 2000 | pmid = 11100619 | pmc = 2560623 }}</ref> Important nutritional measures include the promotion of [[breastfeeding]] and zinc supplementation. While hygienic measures alone may be insufficient for the prevention of [[rotavirus]] diarrhea,<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.rotavirusvaccine.org/documents/WHO_position_paper_rotavirus_2007_000.pdf |title=Rotavirus Vaccine Access and Delivery — PATH |publisher=Rotavirusvaccine.org |date=2011-12-07 |access-date=2013-01-12 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091222043141/http://www.rotavirusvaccine.org/documents/WHO_position_paper_rotavirus_2007_000.pdf |archive-date=2009-12-22 }}</ref> it can be prevented by a safe and potentially cost-effective vaccine.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Valencia-Mendoza A, Bertozzi SM, Gutierrez JP, Itzler R | title = Cost-effectiveness of introducing a rotavirus vaccine in developing countries: the case of Mexico | journal = BMC Infectious Diseases | volume = 8 | article-number = 103 | date = July 2008 | pmid = 18664280 | pmc = 2527317 | doi = 10.1186/1471-2334-8-103 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

==== HIV/AIDS ====
{{Main|HIV|AIDS}}
The HIV/AIDS [[epidemic]] has highlighted the global nature of human health and welfare and globalization has given rise to a trend toward finding common solutions to global health challenges. Numerous international funds have been set up in recent times to address global health challenges such as HIV.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Coovadia HM, Hadingham J | title = HIV/AIDS: global trends, global funds and delivery bottlenecks | journal = Globalization and Health | volume = 1 | article-number = 13 | date = August 2005 | pmid = 16060961 | pmc = 1199613 | doi = 10.1186/1744-8603-1-13 | doi-access = free }}</ref> Since the beginning of the epidemic, more than 70 million people have been infected with the HIV virus and about 35 million people have died of HIV. Globally, 36.9 million [31.1–43.9 million] people were living with HIV at the end of 2017. An estimated 0.8% [0.6–0.9%] of adults aged 15–49 years worldwide are living with HIV, although the burden of the epidemic continues to vary considerably between countries and regions. The WHO African region remains most severely affected, with nearly 1 in every 25 adults (4.1%) living with HIV and accounting for nearly two-thirds of the people living with HIV worldwide.<ref>{{Cite web |title=HIV/AIDS |url=https://www.who.int/gho/hiv/en/ |access-date=2018-11-01 |website=World Health Organization }}</ref> Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) is transmitted through unprotected sex, unclean needles, [[blood transfusion]]s, and from mother to child during birth or [[lactation]]. Globally, HIV is primarily spread through [[sexual intercourse]]. The risk-per-exposure with vaginal sex in low-income countries from female to male is 0.38% and male to female is 0.3%.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Estimated HIV transmission risk per exposure for specific activities and events |date=15 May 2020 |url=https://www.aidsmap.com/Estimated-risk-per-exposure/page/1324038/#item1324093}}</ref> The infection damages the immune system, leading to acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) and eventually, death. [[Management of HIV/AIDS|Antiretroviral drugs]] prolong life and delay the onset of AIDS by minimizing the amount of HIV in the body.

==== Malaria ====
{{Main|Malaria}}
Malaria is a mosquito-borne infectious disease caused by the parasites of the genus ''[[Plasmodium]]''. Symptoms may include fever, headaches, chills, muscle aches and nausea. Each year, there are approximately 500 million cases of malaria worldwide, most commonly among children and pregnant women in developing countries.<ref name="Birn">{{cite book | vauthors = Birn A, Pillay Y, Holtz T |url=https://archive.org/details/textbookofintern0000birn |title=Textbook of International Health  |publisher=Oxford University Press |year=2009 |isbn=978-0-19-971985-3 |edition=3rd |page=[https://archive.org/details/textbookofintern0000birn/page/273 273] |url-access=registration}}</ref> The WHO African Region carries a disproportionately high share of the global malaria burden. In 2016, the region was home to 90% of malaria cases and 91% of malaria deaths.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Malaria key facts |url=https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/malaria}}</ref> The use of [[Mosquito net|insecticide-treated bed nets]] is a cost-effective way to reduce deaths from malaria, as is prompt [[artemisinin]]-based combination therapy, supported by [[intermittent preventive therapy]] in pregnancy. International travelers to [[Endemic (epidemiology)|endemic]] zones are advised [[chemoprophylaxis]] with [[antimalarial drugs]] like [[Atovaquone/proguanil|Atovaquone-proguanil]], [[doxycycline]], or [[mefloquine]].<ref>{{Cite web  |publisher= U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention |date=2018-01-26 |title=Malaria – Travelers – Malaria Information and Prophylaxis, by Country |url=https://www.cdc.gov/malaria/travelers/country_table/a.html |access-date=2018-11-01 }}</ref> Global consumption and international trade in deforestation-associated commodities could also indirectly influence malaria risk. Many primary commodities cause deforestation and deforestation can increase malaria transmission. Consumption of such commodities in developed nations could increase malaria risk in developing nations.<ref name="pmid32152272">{{cite journal | vauthors = Chaves LS, Fry J, Malik A, Geschke A, Sallum MA, Lenzen M | title = Global consumption and international trade in deforestation-associated commodities could influence malaria risk | journal = Nature Communications | volume = 11 | issue = 1 | article-number = 1258 | date = March 2020 | pmid = 32152272 | pmc = 7062889 | doi = 10.1038/s41467-020-14954-1  | doi-access = free| bibcode = 2020NatCo..11.1258C }}</ref>

==== Bacterial pathogens ====
[[File:Global number of deaths (A) and YLLs (B), by pathogen and GBD super-region, 2019.jpg|thumb|Global number of deaths (A) and [[Years of potential life lost|YLLs]] (B), by pathogen and [[Global Burden of Disease Study|GBD]] super-region, 2019<ref name="Ikuta_2022"/>]]
[[File:Overall age-standardised mortality rate per 100 000 population for 33 pathogens investigated, 2019.jpg|thumb|Overall age-standardised mortality rate per 100 000 population for 33 pathogens investigated, 2019<ref name="Ikuta_2022"/>]]
A [[Global Burden of Disease Study|GBD study]] reported global estimates of death rates from (33) bacterial pathogens, finding such infections are [[List of causes of death by rate|contributing to one in 8 deaths]] (or ~7.7 million deaths), which {{tooltip|could make it|when "Compared with GBD Level 3 underlying causes of death"}} the second largest cause of death globally in 2019.<ref name="Ikuta_2022">{{cite journal | title = Global mortality associated with 33 bacterial pathogens in 2019: a systematic analysis for the Global Burden of Disease Study 2019 | journal = Lancet | volume = 400 | issue = 10369 | pages = 2221–48 | date = December 2022 | pmid = 36423648 | pmc = 9763654 | doi = 10.1016/S0140-6736(22)02185-7 | doi-access = free | vauthors = Ikuta KS, Swetschinski LR, Robles Aguilar G, Sharara F, Mestrovic T, Gray AP, Davis Weaver N, Wool EE, Han C, Gershberg Hayoon A, Aali A, Abate SM, Abbasi-Kangevari M, Abbasi-Kangevari Z, Abd-Elsalam S, Abebe G, Abedi A, Abhari AP, Abidi H, Aboagye RG, Absalan A, Abubaker Ali H, Acuna JM, Adane TD, Addo IY, Adegboye OA, Adnan M, Adnani QE, Afzal MS, Afzal S | display-authors = 6 | bibcode = 2022Lanc..400.2221I }}</ref>

==== Neglected tropical diseases ====
{{Main|Neglected tropical diseases}}
More than one billion people were treated for at least one neglected tropical disease in 2015.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2017 |title=Unprecedented progress against neglected tropical diseases, WHO reports |url=https://www.who.int/mediacentre/news/releases/2017/ntd-report/en/ |access-date=2017-05-11 |website=World Health Organization }}</ref> For instance, neglected tropical diseases are a diverse group of infectious diseases that are endemic in [[tropical]] and [[Subtropics|subtropical]] regions of 149 countries, primarily effecting low and middle income populations in Africa, Asia, and Latin America. They are variously caused by [[bacteria]] ([[trachoma]], [[leprosy]]), [[virus]]es ([[Dengue fever|dengue]],<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Horstick O, Tozan Y, Wilder-Smith A | title = Reviewing dengue: still a neglected tropical disease? | journal = PLOS Neglected Tropical Diseases | volume = 9 | issue = 4 | article-number = e0003632 | date = April 2015 | pmid = 25928673 | pmc = 4415787 | doi = 10.1371/journal.pntd.0003632 | doi-access = free }}</ref> [[rabies]]), [[protozoa]] ([[African trypanosomiasis|human African trypanosomiasis]], [[Chagas disease|chagas]]), and [[helminths]] ([[schistosomiasis]], [[onchocerciasis]], [[Soil-transmitted helminth|Soil transmitted helminths]]).<ref>{{Cite web |title=Neglected Tropical Diseases — Diseases |url=https://www.cdc.gov/globalhealth/ntd/diseases/index.html |access-date=2017-05-11 |publisher=Centers for Disease Control and Prevention }}</ref> The Global Burden of Disease Study concluded that neglected tropical diseases comprehensively contributed to approximately 26.06 million [[disability-adjusted life year]]s in 2010, as well as significant deleterious economic effects.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Hotez PJ, Alvarado M, Basáñez MG, Bolliger I, Bourne R, Boussinesq M, Brooker SJ, Brown AS, Buckle G, Budke CM, Carabin H, Coffeng LE, Fèvre EM, Fürst T, Halasa YA, Jasrasaria R, Johns NE, Keiser J, King CH, Lozano R, Murdoch ME, O'Hanlon S, Pion SD, Pullan RL, Ramaiah KD, Roberts T, Shepard DS, Smith JL, Stolk WA, Undurraga EA, Utzinger J, Wang M, Murray CJ, Naghavi M | display-authors = 6 | title = The global burden of disease study 2010: interpretation and implications for the neglected tropical diseases | journal = PLOS Neglected Tropical Diseases | volume = 8 | issue = 7 | article-number = e2865 | date = July 2014 | pmid = 25058013 | pmc = 4109880 | doi = 10.1371/journal.pntd.0002865 | doi-access = free }}</ref> In 2011, the World Health Organization launched a 2020 Roadmap for neglected tropical diseases, aiming for the control or elimination of 10 common diseases.<ref>{{Cite book |publisher=World Health Organization |url=https://apps.who.int/iris/bitstream/10665/80245/1/WHO_HTM_NTD_2013.2_eng.pdf |title=Sustaining the drive to overcome the global impact of neglected tropical diseases: second WHO report on neglected tropical diseases; summary |year=2013 |id=WHO/HTM/NTD/2013.2}}</ref> The 2012 [[London Declaration on Neglected Tropical Diseases|London Declaration]] builds on this initiative, and called on endemic countries and the international community to improve access to [[Sustainable Development Goal 6|clean water and basic sanitation]], improved living conditions, [[vector control]], and [[health education]], to reach the 2020 goals.<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://www.who.int/neglected_diseases/London_Declaration_NTDs.pdf?ua=1 |title=London Declaration on Neglected Tropical Diseases |year=2012}}</ref> In 2017, a WHO report cited "unprecedented progress" against neglected tropical diseases since 2007, especially due to [[mass drug administration]] of drugs donated by pharmaceutical companies.<ref>{{Cite book |publisher=World Health Organization |url=https://apps.who.int/iris/bitstream/10665/255011/1/9789241565448-eng.pdf?ua=1 |title=Integrating Neglected Tropical Diseases into Global Health and Development |year=2017 |isbn=978-92-4-156544-8}}</ref>

===Health research and development===
{{See also|Funding of science|Research question#Aggregated research questions and coordination}}
{{Expand section|date=December 2022}}
The global health approach could foster international collaboration in medical research and development and share of its results such as vaccines, optimizing overall global health for citizens. The [[U.S. Agency for International Development]]'s new Global Health Research and Development Strategy 2023–2028 includes plans to coordinate with such stakeholders in support of innovative global health product development and work with other agencies like the [[CDC]] and National Institutes of Health. Another approach to health would be the innovation of [[vaccines]]. The [[Washington Post]] reported the US government's new five billion dollar budget on vaccines to prevent Covid variants because the Vaccines' access and public-private partnerships are important.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Pagliusi S, Ting CC, Lobos F | title = Vaccines: Shaping global health | journal = Vaccine | volume = 35 | issue = 12 | pages = 1579–85 | date = March 2017 | pmid = 28237501 | pmc = 7127343 | doi = 10.1016/j.vaccine.2017.02.017 }}</ref> Often the relevance of mechanisms to stimulate research and development is limited by national scopes and "by the transnational nature of the problem which asks for an international approach".<ref>{{cite web |vauthors=Wernli D, Flahault A |title=Strengthening research and development for and access to health technologies for neglected diseases and global health threats |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/307946372 |date=2015}}</ref> Financing models, creation of evidence-based recommendations, and logistics may be part of that.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Bloom DE, Cadarette D | title = Infectious Disease Threats in the Twenty-First Century: Strengthening the Global Response | journal = Frontiers in Immunology | volume = 10 | article-number = 549 | date = 2019 | pmid = 30984169 | pmc = 6447676 | doi = 10.3389/fimmu.2019.00549 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

A seminal article by [[Thomas Pogge]], published in ''Metaphilosophy'' in 2005, addresses the global [[health crisis]], in which one-third of all human deaths are due to poverty-related causes, the majority of which are preventable. Pogge critiques the existing patent regime, particularly the [[TRIPS agreement]], for its role in limiting access to essential medicines and violating human rights. Pogge proposes a reform of the global health system  with the objective of making medical knowledge freely available as a [[global public good]]. The reform includes providing the results of successful drug development as public goods, rewarding inventor firms based on the impact of their inventions on the global disease burden, and ensuring a fair and feasible allocation of costs. The article argues that this reform would align the interests of pharmaceutical companies with those of patients and generic drug producers, incentivize research into neglected diseases, and be cost-effective. It also discusses the moral urgency of addressing the global health crisis and the responsibility of high-income countries to support reforms that benefit the global poor. It concludes by emphasizing the feasibility and political realism of the proposed reform, which aims to extend the benefits of medical advancements to the poor and realize human rights more fully.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Human Rights and Global Health: A Research Program|last=Pogge|first=Thomas W.|journal=Metaphilosophy|issue=1–2|doi=10.1111/j.1467-9973.2005.00362.x|year=2005|volume=36|pages=182–209|jstor=24439623|doi-access=free}}</ref>

===Maternal health===
{{Main|Maternal health|Reproductive health}}
[[Complications of pregnancy]] and [[childbirth]] are the leading causes of [[maternal mortality|death among women]] of reproductive age. In many developing countries, a woman dies from complications from childbirth approximately every minute.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.unicef.org/mdg/maternal.html|publisher=UNICEF|title=Improve Maternal Health|access-date=2011-07-13|archive-date=2019-03-31|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190331092758/https://www.unicef.org/mdg/maternal.html}}</ref> According to the World Health Organization's 2005 [[World Health Report]], poor maternal conditions are the fourth leading cause of death for women worldwide, after [[HIV/AIDS]], malaria, and tuberculosis.<ref>{{cite web|publisher=World Health Organization|year=2005|title=World Health Report 2005: make every mother and child count|location=Geneva|url=https://www.who.int/whr/2005/en/index.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050409001725/http://www.who.int/whr/2005/en/index.html|archive-date=April 9, 2005}}</ref> Most maternal deaths and injuries can be prevented, and such deaths have been largely eradicated in the [[developed world]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2010/02/100218092852.htm|work=Science Daily|title=Most Maternal Deaths in Sub-Saharan Africa Could Be Avoided|date= 2 March 2010|access-date=3 March 2011}}</ref> Targets for improving maternal health include increasing and assisting the number of deliveries accompanied by skilled [[birth attendant]]s.<ref name=bhutta2008 /> 68 low-income countries tracked by the WHO- and UNICEF-led collaboration ''Countdown to 2015'' are estimated to hold for 97% of worldwide maternal and child deaths.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.countdown2015mnch.org/reports-publications|work=Countdown to 2015|title=Progress reports|access-date=2011-03-15|archive-date=2011-07-25|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110725200507/http://www.countdown2015mnch.org/reports-publications}}</ref>

===Nutrition===
{{Main|Human nutrition|Healthy diet}}
In 2010, about 104 million children were [[underweight]], and undernutrition contributes to about one third of child deaths around the world.<ref>{{cite web|publisher=World Health Organization|work=Nutrition|title=Challenges|url=https://www.who.int/nutrition/challenges/en/index.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060321175818/http://www.who.int/nutrition/challenges/en/index.html|archive-date=March 21, 2006}}</ref> (Undernutrition is not to be confused with ''[[malnutrition]]'', which refers to poor ''proportion'' of food intake and can thus refer to [[obesity]].)<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Shetty P | title=Malnutrition and Undernutrition | journal=Medicine | year=2003 | volume=31 | issue=4 | pages=18–22 | doi=10.1383/medc.31.4.18.27958 | issn=1357-3039 | quote=Malnutrition refers to all deviations from adequate and optimal nutritional status, including energy undernutrition and over-nutrition (obesity is a form of malnutrition). The term 'undernutrition' is used to refer to generally poor nutritional status, but also implies underfeeding}}</ref> Undernutrition impairs the [[immune system]], increasing the frequency, severity, and duration of infections (including [[measles]], [[pneumonia]], and [[diarrhea]]). Infection can further contribute to malnutrition.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Schaible UE, Kaufmann SH | title = Malnutrition and infection: complex mechanisms and global impacts | journal = PLOS Medicine | volume = 4 | issue = 5 | article-number = e115 | date = May 2007 | pmid = 17472433 | pmc = 1858706 | doi = 10.1371/journal.pmed.0040115 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

[[Micronutrient deficiency|Deficiencies]] of [[micronutrient]]s, such as [[vitamin A]], [[iron]], [[iodine]], and [[zinc]], are common worldwide and can compromise intellectual potential, growth, development, and adult productivity.<ref>{{cite web|publisher=World Health Organization|url=https://www.who.int/vaccines/en/vitamina.shtml|title=Vitamin A supplementation|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130125025617/http://www.who.int/vaccines/en/vitamina.shtml|archive-date=2013-01-25 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Stevens GA, Beal T, Mbuya MN, Luo H, Neufeld LM | title = Micronutrient deficiencies among preschool-aged children and women of reproductive age worldwide: a pooled analysis of individual-level data from population-representative surveys | journal = The Lancet. Global Health | volume = 10 | issue = 11 | pages = e1590–9 | date = November 2022 | pmid = 36240826 | doi = 10.1016/S2214-109X(22)00367-9 | s2cid = 252857990 | doi-access = free | pmc = 10918648 | bibcode = 2022LanGH..10e1590S }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Lynch S, Stoltzfus R, Rawat R | title = Critical review of strategies to prevent and control iron deficiency in children | journal = Food and Nutrition Bulletin | volume = 28 | issue = 4 Suppl | pages = S610–S620 | date = December 2007 | pmid = 18297898 | doi = 10.1177/15648265070284S413 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref name="thelancet.com">{{cite journal | vauthors = Walker SP, Wachs TD, Gardner JM, Lozoff B, Wasserman GA, Pollitt E, Carter JA | title = Child development: risk factors for adverse outcomes in developing countries | journal = Lancet | volume = 369 | issue = 9556 | pages = 145–157 | date = January 2007 | pmid = 17223478 | doi = 10.1016/S0140-6736(07)60076-2 | bibcode = 2007Lanc..369..145W | s2cid = 11120228 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Lazzerini M | title = Effect of zinc supplementation on child mortality | journal = Lancet | volume = 370 | issue = 9594 | pages = 1194–5 | date = October 2007 | pmid = 17920908 | doi = 10.1016/S0140-6736(07)61524-4 | s2cid = 33297518 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Fischer Walker CL, Ezzati M, Black RE | title = Global and regional child mortality and burden of disease attributable to zinc deficiency | journal = European Journal of Clinical Nutrition | volume = 63 | issue = 5 | pages = 591–7 | date = May 2009 | pmid = 18270521 | doi = 10.1038/ejcn.2008.9 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Lazzerini M, Wanzira H | title = Oral zinc for treating diarrhoea in children | journal = The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | volume = 12 | issue = 12 | article-number = CD005436 | date = December 2016 | pmid = 27996088 | pmc = 5450879 | doi = 10.1002/14651858.CD005436.pub5 }}</ref> Interventions to prevent malnutrition include micronutrient supplementation, [[Food fortification|fortification]] of basic grocery foods, dietary diversification, hygienic measures to reduce spread of infections, and the promotion of [[breastfeeding]].

=== Non-communicable diseases ===
{{Main|Non-communicable disease}}
Approximately 80% of deaths linked to [[non-communicable disease]]s occur in developing countries.<ref>{{cite web |year=2011 |title=WHO: Global Status Report on Noncommunicable Diseases 2010 |url=https://www.who.int/nmh/publications/ncd_report2010/en/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110430112742/http://www.who.int/nmh/publications/ncd_report2010/en/ |archive-date=April 30, 2011}}</ref> For instance, [[urbanization]] and [[Ageing|aging]] have led to increasing poor health conditions related to non-communicable diseases in India. Similarly, China's rapid urbanization and modernization have been associated with increased sedentary lifestyles, contributing to the rise in NCDs in the region.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Menhas R, Dai J, Ashraf MA, M Noman S, Khurshid S, Mahmood S, Weng Y, Ahmad Laar R, Sang X, Kamran M, Shahzad B, Iqbal W | display-authors = 6 | title = Physical Inactivity, Non-Communicable Diseases and National Fitness Plan of China for Physical Activity | journal = Risk Management and Healthcare Policy | volume = 14 | pages = 2319–31 | date = 2021-06-03 | pmid = 34113188 | pmc = 8184286 | doi = 10.2147/RMHP.S258660 | doi-access = free }}</ref> The fastest-growing causes of disease burden over the last 26 years were [[diabetes]] (rate increased by 80%) and [[Ischemic Heart Disease|ischemic heart disease]] (up 34%). More than 60% of deaths, about 6.1 million, in 2016 were due to NCDs, up from about 38% in 1990.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2017-11-13 |title=Comprehensive health study in India finds rise of non-communicable diseases |url=http://www.healthdata.org/news-release/comprehensive-health-study-india-finds-rise-non-communicable-diseases |access-date=2018-11-01 |archive-date=2023-02-09 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230209235129/https://www.healthdata.org/news-release/comprehensive-health-study-india-finds-rise-non-communicable-diseases }}</ref> Increases in [[Refugee|refugee urbanization]], has led to a growing number of people diagnosed with chronic non-communicable diseases.<ref name="amara">{{cite journal | vauthors = Amara AH, Aljunid SM | title = Noncommunicable diseases among urban refugees and asylum-seekers in developing countries: a neglected health care need | journal = Globalization and Health | volume = 10 | page = 24 | date = April 2014 | pmid = 24708876 | pmc = 3978000 | doi = 10.1186/1744-8603-10-24 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

In September 2011, the United Nations is hosting its first General Assembly Special Summit on the issue of non-communicable diseases.<ref>{{cite web |date=13 May 2010 |title=Press Conference on General Assembly Decision to Convene Summit in September 2011 on Non-Communicable Diseases |url=https://www.un.org/News/briefings/docs//2010/100513_Diseases.doc.htm |publisher=United Nations |location=New York}}</ref> Noting that non-communicable diseases are the cause of some 35 million deaths each year, the international community is being increasingly called to take measures for the prevention and control of chronic diseases and mitigate their impacts on the world population, especially on women, who are usually the [[Caregiver|primary caregivers]].

For example, the rate of [[Diabetes mellitus|type 2 diabetes]], associated with [[obesity]], has been on the rise in countries previously troubled by hunger. In low-income countries, the number of individuals with diabetes is expected to increase from 84 million to 228 million by 2030.<ref name="nejm">{{cite journal | vauthors = Hossain P, Kawar B, El Nahas M | title = Obesity and diabetes in the developing world--a growing challenge | journal = The New England Journal of Medicine | volume = 356 | issue = 3 | pages = 213–5 | date = January 2007 | pmid = 17229948 | doi = 10.1056/NEJMp068177 | doi-access = free }}</ref> Obesity, a preventable condition, is associated with numerous chronic diseases, including [[Cardiovascular disease|cardiovascular conditions]], [[stroke]], certain [[cancer]]s, and [[respiratory disease]]. About 16% of the global burden of disease, measured as DALYs, has been accounted for by obesity.<ref name="nejm" />

Considering that 360 million people across the world live with disabling hearing loss, including 32 million children and nearly 180 million older adults, and that chronic ear diseases, such as chronic suppurative otitis media, can lead to hearing loss and may cause life-threatening complications, the seventieth World Health Assembly on May 31, 2017 signed the resolution WHA70.13 (Agenda item 15.8)  urging member states to integrate strategies for ear and hearing care within the framework of their primary health care systems, under the umbrella of universal health coverage.<ref>{{cite web |title=Agenda item 15.8: Prevention of deafness and hearing loss |date=31 May 2017 |work=Seventieth World Health Assembly |id=WHA70.13 |url=https://apps.who.int/gb/ebwha/pdf_files/WHA70/A70_R13-en.pdf}}</ref>  A World Report on Hearing (WRH) was published in response to the resolution (WHA70.13), to provide guidance for Member States to integrate ear and hearing care into their national health plans.<ref>{{Cite book |title=World report on hearing |date=2021 |publisher=World Health Organization |isbn=978-92-4-002048-1 |location=Geneva |oclc=1295473345}}</ref>

=== Violence against women ===
{{Main|Domestic violence}}

[[Violence against women]] has been defined as: "physical, sexual and psychological violence occurring in the family and in the general community, including [[battery (crime)|battering]], [[sexual abuse]], [[Dowry|dowry-related]] violence, [[rape]], [[female genital mutilation]] and other traditional practices harmful to women, non-spousal violence and violence related to exploitation, [[sexual harassment]] and [[intimidation]] at work, in educational institutions and elsewhere, [[Human trafficking|trafficking]] in women, forced [[prostitution]] and violence perpetrated or condoned by the state."<ref>{{cite web|publisher=The United Nations Population Fund|year=2005|title=Violence Against Women Fact Sheet|url=http://www.unfpa.org/swp/2005/presskit/factsheets/facts_vaw.htm|access-date=2012-09-29|archive-date=2012-09-08|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120908112509/http://www.unfpa.org/swp/2005/presskit/factsheets/facts_vaw.htm}}</ref> In addition to causing injury, violence may increase "women's long-term risk of a number of other health problems, including [[chronic pain]], [[physical disability]], [[Substance abuse|drug and alcohol abuse]], and [[Depression (mood)|depression]]".<ref>{{cite book |last1=Ellsberg |first1=M. |last2=Heise |first2=L. |title=Researching Violence Against Women: A Practical Guide for Researchers and Activists |publisher=World Health Organization, PATH |date=2005 |isbn=92-4-154647-6 |url=https://iris.who.int/bitstream/handle/10665/42966/9241546476_eng.pdf}}</ref> The WHO Report on global and regional estimates on violence against women found that partner abuse causes women to have 16% more chances of suffering [[miscarriage]]s, 41% more occurrences of [[Preterm birth|pre-term birth]] babies and twice the likeliness of having [[abortion]]s and acquiring HIV or other [[Sexually transmitted infection|STDs]]<ref>{{cite book |publisher=World Health Organization |hdl=10665/85239 |title=Global and regional estimates of violence against women: prevalence and health effects of intimate partner violence and non-partner sexual violence |isbn=978-92-4-156462-5 |year=2013 }}</ref>

Although statistics can be difficult to obtain as many cases go unreported, it is estimated that one in every five women faces some form of violence during her lifetime, in some cases leading to serious injury or even death.<ref>{{cite report | title = Addressing violence against women and achieving the Millennium Development Goals | location = Geneva, Switzerland | work = World Health Organization | date = September 2005 | url = https://apps.who.int/iris/bitstream/handle/10665/43361/?sequence=1 |id=WHO/FCH/GWH/05.1}}</ref> Risk factors for being an offender include low education, past exposure to [[Child Maltreatment|child maltreatment]] or witnessing violence between parents, harmful use of alcohol, attitudes accepting of violence, and [[gender inequality]].<ref>{{cite web|publisher=World Health Organization|year=2011|title=Violence against women: Intimate partner and sexual violence against women fact sheet|url=https://www.who.int/mediacentre/factsheets/fs239/en/}}</ref> Equality of women has been addressed in the [[Millennium Development Goals]]. Now, [[gender equality]] is [[Sustainable Development Goal 5]]. Preventing the violence against women needs to form an essential part of the public health reforms in the form of [[Advocacy|advocation]] and [[Evidence-based practice|evidence gathering]]. [[Preventive healthcare|Primary prevention]] in the form of raising [[Women's empowerment|women economic empowerment]] facilities, [[microfinance]] and skills training social projects related to gender equality should be conducted.

Activities promoting relationship and communication skills among couples, reducing alcohol access and altering societal ideologies should be organized. Childhood interventions, community and school-based education, raising media-oriented awareness and other approaches should be carried out to challenge social norms and [[Stereotype|stereotypical]] thought processes to promote [[Behavior change (public health)|behavioral change]] among men and raise gender equality. Trained health care providers would play a vital role in secondary and tertiary prevention of abuse by performing early identification of women suffering from violence and contributing to the addressing of their health and psychological needs. They could be highly important in prevention of the recurrence of violence and the mitigation of its effects on the health of the abused women and their children.<ref>{{cite book | vauthors = | chapter = | pages = | veditors = Cockerham WC, Quah SR |title=International Encyclopedia of Public Health | edition = Second |date=2017 |publisher=Elsevier/AP | isbn = 978-0-12-803708-9 }}</ref>
The Member States of the World Health Assembly endorsed a plan in 2016 for reinforcing the health system's role in addressing the global phenomenon of violence against women and girls and working towards their health and protection.<ref>{{cite web |last1=WHO |url=https://www.who.int/reproductivehealth/topics/violence/action-plan-endorsement/en/ |website=WHO.int |access-date=1 December 2019 |title=The World Health Assembly endorses the global plan of action on violence against women and girls, and also against children}}</ref>

===Global surgery===
[[Halfdan T. Mahler]], the 3rd Director-General of the [[World Health Organization]] (WHO), first brought attention to the disparities in surgery and surgical care when he stated, "the vast majority of the world's population has no access whatsoever to skilled surgical care and little is being done to find a solution".<ref>{{cite report | vauthors = Mahler H | title = Address by Dr. H. Mahler, Director General of the World Health Organization, in presenting his report for 1986 and 1987 | work = Forty-first World Health Assembly: world health-2000 and beyond. | jstor = 41989284 }}</ref>

While significant progresses have been made in fields within global health such as [[Neglected tropical diseases|infectious diseases]], [[Maternal health|maternal and child health]], and even other [[non-communicable diseases]] over the past several decades, the provision of [[Surgery|surgery and surgical care]] in resource-limited settings have largely remained unmet with about 5 billion people lacking access to safe and affordable surgical and anesthesia care.<ref name=Meara15/> This is especially true in the poorest countries, which account for over one-third of the population but only 3.5% of all surgeries that occur worldwide.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Weiser TG, Regenbogen SE, Thompson KD, Haynes AB, Lipsitz SR, Berry WR, Gawande AA | title = An estimation of the global volume of surgery: a modelling strategy based on available data | journal = Lancet | volume = 372 | issue = 9633 | pages = 139–144 | date = July 2008 | pmid = 18582931 | doi = 10.1016/S0140-6736(08)60878-8 | s2cid = 17918156 }}</ref> In fact, it has been estimated that up to 30% of the total [[Disease burden|global burden of disease (GBD)]] could be attributable to surgical conditions, which include a mix of [[Injury|injuries]], [[malignancies]], [[congenital anomalies]], and [[complications of pregnancy]].<ref name=McQueen10>{{cite journal | vauthors = McQueen KA, Ozgediz D, Riviello R, Hsia RY, Jayaraman S, Sullivan SR, Meara JG | title = Essential surgery: Integral to the right to health | journal = Health and Human Rights | volume = 12 | issue = 1 | pages = 137–152 | date = June 2010 | pmid = 20930260 | url = https://www.hhrjournal.org/2013/08/essential-surgery-integral-to-the-right-to-health/ }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Shrime MG, Bickler SW, Alkire BC, Mock C | title = Global burden of surgical disease: an estimation from the provider perspective | journal = The Lancet. Global Health | volume = 3 | issue = Suppl 2 | pages = S8–S9 | date = April 2015 | pmid = 25926322 | doi = 10.1016/S2214-109X(14)70384-5 | doi-access = free }}</ref>  As a result, global surgery has become an emerging field within global health as "the [[Academic discipline#Multidisciplinary|multidisciplinary]] enterprise of providing improved and equitable surgical care to the world's population, with its core belief as the issues of need, access and quality" and has often been described as the "neglected stepchild of global health", a term coined by [[Paul Farmer|Dr. Paul Farmer]] to highlight the urgent need for further work in this area.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Bath M, Bashford T, Fitzgerald JE | title = What is 'global surgery'? Defining the multidisciplinary interface between surgery, anaesthesia and public health | journal = BMJ Global Health | volume = 4 | issue = 5 | article-number = e001808 | year = 2019 | pmid = 31749997 | pmc = 6830053 | doi = 10.1136/bmjgh-2019-001808 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Farmer PE, Kim JY | title = Surgery and global health: a view from beyond the OR | journal = World Journal of Surgery | volume = 32 | issue = 4 | pages = 533–6 | date = April 2008 | pmid = 18311574 | pmc = 2267857 | doi = 10.1007/s00268-008-9525-9 }}</ref> Furthermore, [[Jim Yong Kim|Jim Young Kim]], the former President of the [[World Bank]], proclaimed in 2014 that "surgery is an indivisible, indispensable part of health care and of progress towards universal health coverage."<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Dare AJ, Grimes CE, Gillies R, Greenberg SL, Hagander L, Meara JG, Leather AJ | title = Global surgery: defining an emerging global health field | journal = Lancet | volume = 384 | issue = 9961 | pages = 2245–7 | date = December 2014 | pmid = 24853601 | doi = 10.1016/S0140-6736(14)60237-3 | s2cid = 37349469 }}</ref>

In 2015, the Lancet Commission on Global Surgery (LCoGS) published the landmark report titled "Global Surgery 2030: evidence and solutions for achieving health, welfare, and economic development", describing the large, pre-existing burden of surgical diseases in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) and future directions for increasing universal access to safe surgery by the year 2030.<ref name=Meara15>{{cite journal | vauthors = Meara JG, Leather AJ, Hagander L, Alkire BC, Alonso N, Ameh EA, Bickler SW, Conteh L, Dare AJ, Davies J, Mérisier ED, El-Halabi S, Farmer PE, Gawande A, Gillies R, Greenberg SL, Grimes CE, Gruen RL, Ismail EA, Kamara TB, Lavy C, Lundeg G, Mkandawire NC, Raykar NP, Riesel JN, Rodas E, Rose J, Roy N, Shrime MG, Sullivan R, Verguet S, Watters D, Weiser TG, Wilson IH, Yamey G, Yip W | display-authors = 6 | title = Global Surgery 2030: evidence and solutions for achieving health, welfare, and economic development | journal = Lancet | volume = 386 | issue = 9993 | pages = 569–624 | date = August 2015 | pmid = 25924834 | doi = 10.1016/S0140-6736(15)60160-X | s2cid = 2048403 | doi-access = free }}</ref> The Commission highlighted that 143 million additional procedures were needed every year to prevent further [[morbidity]] and [[Mortality rate|mortality]] from treatable surgical conditions as well as a $12.3 trillion loss in economic productivity by the year 2030.<ref name=Meara15 /> It emphasized the need to significantly improve the capacity for Bellwether procedures — [[laparotomy]], [[caesarean section]], [[open fracture|open fracture care]] — which are considered a minimum level of care that first-level hospitals should be able to provide in order to capture the most basic emergency surgical care.<ref name=Meara15 /><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = O'Neill KM, Greenberg SL, Cherian M, Gillies RD, Daniels KM, Roy N, Raykar NP, Riesel JN, Spiegel D, Watters DA, Gruen RL | display-authors = 6 | title = Bellwether Procedures for Monitoring and Planning Essential Surgical Care in Low- and Middle-Income Countries: Caesarean Delivery, Laparotomy, and Treatment of Open Fractures | journal = World Journal of Surgery | volume = 40 | issue = 11 | pages = 2611–9 | date = November 2016 | pmid = 27351714 | doi = 10.1007/s00268-016-3614-y | publisher = Springer Science and Business Media LLC | s2cid = 12830913 }}</ref> In order to address these challenges and track progress, the Commission defined the following core indicators for assessing access to safe and affordable surgical d anesthesia care:<ref name=Meara15 />
{| class="wikitable"
|+
!Core Indicators
!Definition
!Target
|-
|Access to timely essential surgery
|The proportion of the population that can access, within 2 hours, a facility that can do cesarean delivery, laparotomy, and treatment of open fracture (the Bellwether Procedures)
|A minimum of 80% coverage of essential surgical and anesthesia services per country by 2030
|-
|Specialist surgical workforce density
|The number of specialist surgical, anaesthetic, and obstetric physicians who are working, per 100,000 population
|100% of countries with at least 20 surgical, anaesthetic, and obstetric physicians per 100,000 population by 2030
|-
|Surgical volume
|The number of procedures done in an operating theatre, per 100,000 population per year
|80% of countries by 2020 and 100% of countries by 2030 tracking surgical volume; a minimum of 5000 procedures per 100,000 population by 2030
|-
|Perioperative mortality
|All-cause death rate before discharge in patients who have undergone a procedure in an operating theatre, divided by the total number of procedures, presented as a percentage
|80% of countries by 2020 and 100% of countries by 2030 tracking perioperative mortality; in 2020, assess global data and set national targets for 2030
|-
|Protection against impoverishing expenditure
|The proportion of households protected against impoverishment from direct out-of-pocket payments for surgical and anesthesia care
|100% protection against impoverishment from out-of-pocket payments for surgical and anaesthesia care by 2030
|-
|Protection against catastrophic expenditure
|The proportion of households protected against catastrophic expenditure from direct out-of-pocket payments for surgical and anesthesia care
|100% protection against catastrophic expenditure from out-of-pocket payments for surgical and anaesthesia care by 2030
|}
Meeting these goals by the year 2030 would require increases in [[anesthetist]]s, [[obstetricians]], [[surgeon]]s, [[Nursing|nurses]], and facilities with [[Operating theater|operating rooms]] as well as pre- and post-surgical care capacities.

Data from WHO and the World Bank indicate that scaling up infrastructure to enable access to surgical care in regions where it is currently limited or is non-existent is a low-cost measure relative to the significant morbidity and mortality caused by lack of surgical treatment.<ref name=McQueen10 /> In fact, a systematic review found that the [[Cost-effectiveness|cost-effectiveness ratio]] — dollars spent per DALYs averted — for surgical interventions is on par or exceeds those of major public health interventions such as [[oral rehydration therapy]], [[breastfeeding promotion]], and even [[Management of HIV/AIDS|HIV/AIDS antiretroviral therapy]].<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Chao TE, Sharma K, Mandigo M, Hagander L, Resch SC, Weiser TG, Meara JG | title = Cost-effectiveness of surgery and its policy implications for global health: a systematic review and analysis | journal = The Lancet. Global Health | volume = 2 | issue = 6 | pages = e334–45 | date = June 2014 | pmid = 25103302 | doi = 10.1016/S2214-109X(14)70213-X | doi-access = free }}</ref> This finding challenged the common misconception that surgical care is financially prohibitive endeavor not worth pursuing in LMICs.

In terms of the financial impact on the patients, the lack of adequate surgical and anesthesia care has resulted in 33 million individuals every year facing catastrophic health expenditure — the out-of-pocket healthcare cost exceeding 40% of a given household's income.<ref name=Meara15 /><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Xu K, Evans DB, Kawabata K, Zeramdini R, Klavus J, Murray CJ | title = Household catastrophic health expenditure: a multicountry analysis | journal = Lancet | volume = 362 | issue = 9378 | pages = 111–7 | date = July 2003 | pmid = 12867110 | doi = 10.1016/S0140-6736(03)13861-5 | s2cid = 2052830 }}</ref>

In alignment with the LCoGS call for action, the [[World Health Assembly]] adopted the resolution WHA68.15 in 2015 that stated, "Strengthening emergency and essential surgical care and anesthesia as a component of universal health coverage."<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Price R, Makasa E, Hollands M | title = World Health Assembly Resolution WHA68.15: "Strengthening Emergency and Essential Surgical Care and Anesthesia as a Component of Universal Health Coverage"—Addressing the Public Health Gaps Arising from Lack of Safe, Affordable and Accessible Surgical and Anesthetic Services | journal = World Journal of Surgery | volume = 39 | issue = 9 | pages = 2115–25 | date = September 2015 | pmid = 26239773 | doi = 10.1007/s00268-015-3153-y | s2cid = 13027859 }}</ref> This not only mandated the WHO to prioritize strengthening the surgical and anesthesia care globally, but also led to governments of the member states recognizing the urgent need for increasing capacity in surgery and anesthesia. Additionally, the third edition of [[Disease Control Priorities Project|Disease Control Priorities]] (DCP3), published in 2015 by the [[World Bank]], declared surgery as essential and featured an entire volume dedicated to building surgical capacity.<ref>{{Cite book | vauthors = Debas HT, Donkor P, Gawande A, Jamison DT, Kruk ME, Mock CN | veditors = Debas HT, Donkor P, Gawande A, Jamison DT, Kruk ME, Mock CN |date=2015-03-24 |title=Disease Control Priorities | edition = 3rd | volume = 1 Essential Surgery |doi=10.1596/978-1-4648-0346-8 |pmid=26740991 |hdl=10986/21568 |url=https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/handle/10986/21568 | isbn = 978-1-4648-0367-3 }}</ref>

A key policy framework that arose from this renewed global commitment towards surgical care worldwide is the National Surgical Obstetric and Anesthesia Plan (NSOAP).<ref name=Truch20>{{cite journal | vauthors = Truché P, Shoman H, Reddy CL, Jumbam DT, Ashby J, Mazhiqi A, Wurdeman T, Ameh EA, Smith M, Lugazia E, Makasa E, Park KB, Meara JG | display-authors = 6 | title = Globalization of national surgical, obstetric and anesthesia plans: the critical link between health policy and action in global surgery | journal = Globalization and Health | volume = 16 | issue = 1 | article-number = 1 | date = January 2020 | pmid = 31898532 | pmc = 6941290 | doi = 10.1186/s12992-019-0531-5 | doi-access = free }}</ref> NSOAP focuses on policy-to-action capacity building for surgical care with tangible steps as follows: (1) analysis of baseline indicators, (2) partnership with local champions, (3) broad stakeholder engagement, (4) consensus building and synthesis of ideas, (5) language refinement, (6) costing, (7) dissemination, and (8) implementation. This approach has been widely adopted and has served as guiding principles between international collaborators and local institutions and governments. Successful implementations have allowed for sustainability in terms of longterm monitoring, quality improvement, and continued political and financial support.<ref name=Truch20 />

====The NIHR Global Health Research Unit on Global Surgery====
Seven surgical research Hubs in [[Benin]], [[Ghana]], [[India]], [[Mexico]], [[Nigeria]], [[Rwanda]] and [[South Africa]] with an extensive network of urban and rural 'Spoke' hospitals have joined to create the NIHR.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.globalsurgeryunit.org/ |title=NIHR Global Health Research Unit on Global Surgery  |website=The NIHR Global Health Research Unit on Global Surgery }}</ref> The NIHR Global Health Research Unit on Global Surgery is led by the [[University of Birmingham]]<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.globalsurgeryunit.org/global-surgery-our-teams/university-of-birmingham/ |title= NIHR Global Health Research Unit on Global Surgery — University of Birmingham | website=The NIHR Global Health Research Unit on Global Surgery }}</ref> which provides overall oversight in relation to the Unit strategy, infrastructure and delivery, research and finance.

The network prioritized surgical topics that needed research and has performed multiple surgical studies. The network resulted in many research groups including GlobalSurg I, II, III<ref>{{cite web |url=https://globalsurg.org/who-we-are/ |title= About GlobalSurg |website=GlobalSurg |access-date= January 28, 2023}}</ref> and COVIDSurg<ref>{{cite web |url=https://globalsurg.org/covidsurg/ |title=CovidSurg  |date=April 30, 2005 |website=GlobalSurg|access-date=January 28, 2023}}</ref> and many other trials with worldwide collaborations as project FALCON,<ref>{{cite journal |author=NIHR Global Research Health Unit on Global Surgery |date=October 25, 2021 |title=Reducing surgical site infections in low-income and middle-income countries (FALCON): a pragmatic, multicentre, stratified, randomised controlled trial |journal=Lancet |volume=398 |issue=10312 |pages=1687–99 |doi=10.1016/S0140-6736(21)01548-8 |pmc=8586736  |pmid=34710362 }}</ref> CHEETAH<ref>{{cite journal |author=NIHR Global Research Health Unit on Global Surgery

====Other global surgery collaborations====
More trials have emerged to assess surgical outcomes around the World using big data from thousands of centers. Other notable trials include:

* Global PaedSurg; The study was published in The Lancet examined the risk of mortality for nearly 4000 babies born with birth defects in 264 hospitals around the world. The study found babies born with birth defects involving the intestinal tract have a two in five chance of dying in a low-income country compared to one in five in a middle-income country and one in twenty in a high-income country.<ref>{{cite journal 
|author=Global PaedSurg Research Collaboration 
|date=July 13, 2021
|title=Mortality from gastrointestinal congenital anomalies at 264 hospitals in 74 low-income, middle-income, and high-income countries: a multicentre, international, prospective cohort study
|journal=Lancet |volume=398 |issue=10297 |pages=325–339 |doi=10.1016/S0140-6736(18)30001-1 |pmid=34270932 |pmc=8314066 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://frenchplanete.fr/sante/la-geographie-determine-la-survie-des-bebes-nes-avec-des-malformations-congenitales-a-travers-le-monde/ |title=La géographie détermine la survie des bébés nés avec des malformations congénitales à travers le monde |website=FrenchPlanete|date=26 July 2021 }}</ref>
* APORG:  The African Perioperative Research Group (APORG) was launched in South Africa
* ASOS and ASOS-2: The studies showed that death after surgery is a major public health problem in Africa. Surgical patients in Africa are twice as likely to die in hospital following surgery when compared to the global average.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.sunshineslate.com/health/landmark-trial-concludes-to-address-the-problem-of-post-operative-death-in-africa/ |title=Landmark Trial Concludes to address the problem of Post-operative Death in Africa |date= August 26, 2021 |website=SunsineSlate}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Biccard BM, Madiba TE, Kluyts HL, Munlemvo DM, Madzimbamuto FD, Basenero A, Gordon CS, Youssouf C, Rakotoarison SR, Gobin V, Samateh AL, Sani CM, Omigbodun AO, Amanor-Boadu SD, Tumukunde JT, Esterhuizen TM, Manach YL, Forget P, Elkhogia AM, Mehyaoui RM, Zoumeno E, Ndayisaba G, Ndasi H, Ndonga AK, Ngumi ZW, Patel UP, Ashebir DZ, Antwi-Kusi AA, Mbwele B, Sama HD, Elfiky M, Fawzy MA, Pearse RM | display-authors = 6 | title = Perioperative patient outcomes in the African Surgical Outcomes Study: a 7-day prospective observational cohort study | journal = Lancet | volume = 391 | issue = 10130 | pages = 1589–98 | date = April 2018 | pmid = 29306587 | doi = 10.1016/S0140-6736(18)30001-1 | collaboration = African Surgical Outcomes Study (ASOS) investigators. | s2cid = 4666606 | url = https://qmro.qmul.ac.uk/xmlui/handle/123456789/51443 }}</ref>
* ASOS PaedSurg: African Pediatric postoperative outcomes are poor, with up to 4x morbidity and 11x mortality rates than high income countries.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Torborg |first1=Alexandra |last2=Meyer |first2=Heidi |last3=Fiky |first3=Mahmoud El |last4=Fawzy |first4=Maher |last5=Elhadi |first5=Muhammed |last6=Ademuyiwa |first6=Adesoji O. |last7=Osinaike |first7=Babatunde Babasola |last8=Hewitt-Smith |first8=Adam |last9=Nabukenya |first9=Mary T. |last10=Bisegerwa |first10=Ronald |last11=Bouaoud |first11=Souad |last12=Abdoun |first12=Meriem |last13=Adib |first13=Ahmed Rhassane El |last14=Belachew |first14=Fitsum Kifle |last15=Gebre |first15=Meseret |date=2024-04-13 |title=Outcomes after surgery for children in Africa (ASOS-Paeds): a 14-day prospective observational cohort study |url=https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(24)00103-X/abstract |journal=The Lancet |language=English |volume=403 |issue=10435 |pages=1482–1492 |doi=10.1016/S0140-6736(24)00103-X |issn=0140-6736 |pmid=38527482|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
* ACCCOS: COVID-19 Mortality was higher in Africa than reported from studies done in other parts of the World.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Biccard |first1=Bruce M. |last2=Gopalan |first2=Pragasan Dean |last3=Miller |first3=Malcolm |last4=Michell |first4=William Lance |last5=Thomson |first5=David |last6=Ademuyiwa |first6=Adesoji |last7=Aniteye |first7=Ernest |last8=Calligaro |first8=Greg |last9=Chaibou |first9=Maman Sani |last10=Dhufera |first10=Hailu Tamiru |last11=Elfagieh |first11=Mohamed |last12=Elfiky |first12=Mahmoud |last13=Elhadi |first13=Muhammed |last14=Fawzy |first14=Maher |last15=Fredericks |first15=David |date=2021-05-22 |title=Patient care and clinical outcomes for patients with COVID-19 infection admitted to African high-care or intensive care units (ACCCOS): a multicentre, prospective, observational cohort study |journal=The Lancet |language=English |volume=397 |issue=10288 |pages=1885–1894 |doi=10.1016/S0140-6736(21)00441-4 |issn=0140-6736 |pmid=34022988|pmc=8137309 }}</ref>
