Another systematic review analyzed pharmacist intervention in smoking cessation and alcohol and weight interventions.<ref name=":2">{{cite journal | vauthors = Brown TJ, Todd A, O'Malley C, Moore HJ, Husband AK, Bambra C, Kasim A, Sniehotta FF, Steed L, Smith S, Nield L, Summerbell CD | title = Community pharmacy-delivered interventions for public health priorities: a systematic review of interventions for alcohol reduction, smoking cessation and weight management, including meta-analysis for smoking cessation | journal = BMJ Open | volume = 6 | issue = 2 | article-number = e009828 | date = February 2016 | pmid = 26928025 | pmc = 4780058 | doi = 10.1136/bmjopen-2015-009828 | doi-access = free }}</ref> They found that evidence suggests that the longer the duration of pharmacist-led intervention, the more influential the attempt at quitting was<ref name=":2"/> In addition, they found that community pharmacists were beneficial in delivering public health information. Pharmacists have a great reach in the community to help with smoking cessation and have proven to help with lifestyle modifications and proper NRT use.<ref name=":2"/>

=== Digital interventions ===

* Interactive web-based and stand-alone computer programs and online communities assist participants in quitting. For example, "quit meters" keep track of statistics such as how long a person has remained abstinent.<ref>{{cite web |vauthors=Hendrick B |title=Computer is an ally in quit-smoking fight |url=https://www.webmd.com/smoking-cessation/news/20090526/computer-is-an-ally-in-quit-smoking-fight |website=WebMD}}</ref> Computerised and interactive tailored interventions may be promising,<ref name="USDHHS2008" />{{rp|93–94}} however, the evidence base for such interventions is weak.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Myung SK, McDonnell DD, Kazinets G, Seo HG, Moskowitz JM | title = Effects of Web- and computer-based smoking cessation programs: meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials | journal = Archives of Internal Medicine | volume = 169 | issue = 10 | pages = 929–937 | date = May 2009 | pmid = 19468084 | doi = 10.1001/archinternmed.2009.109 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Taylor GM, Dalili MN, Semwal M, Civljak M, Sheikh A, Car J | title = Internet-based interventions for smoking cessation | journal = The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | volume = 2017 | issue = 9 | article-number = CD007078 | date = September 2017 | pmid = 28869775 | pmc = 6703145 | doi = 10.1002/14651858.CD007078.pub5 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Hutton HE, Wilson LM, Apelberg BJ, Tang EA, Odelola O, Bass EB, Chander G | title = A systematic review of randomized controlled trials: Web-based interventions for smoking cessation among adolescents, college students, and adults | journal = Nicotine & Tobacco Research | volume = 13 | issue = 4 | pages = 227–238 | date = April 2011 | pmid = 21350042 | doi = 10.1093/ntr/ntq252 | doi-access = free }}</ref>
* A [[MHealth|mobile phone-based intervention]] where automated, supportive text messages are sent alongside other forms of support helps more people quit smoking: "The current evidence supports a beneficial impact of mobile phone-based cessation interventions on six-month cessation outcomes."<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Whittaker R, McRobbie H, Bullen C, Rodgers A, Gu Y | title = Mobile phone-based interventions for smoking cessation | journal = The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | volume = 4 | issue = 4 | article-number = CD006611 | date = April 2016 | pmid = 27060875 | pmc = 6485940 | doi = 10.1002/14651858.CD006611.pub4 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |date=2020-02-12 |title=Text messaging support helps smokers quit, but apps not yet shown to work |url=https://evidence.nihr.ac.uk/alert/text-messaging-support-helps-smokers-quit-but-apps-not-yet-shown-to-work |journal=NIHR Evidence |type=Plain English summary |publisher=National Institute for Health and Care Research |doi=10.3310/signal-000876|s2cid=241974258 |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |title=What is digital health technology and what can it do for me? |website=NIHR Evidence |year=2022 |url=https://evidence.nihr.ac.uk/collection/what-is-digital-health-technology/ |doi=10.3310/nihrevidence_53447 |s2cid=252584020|url-access=subscription }}</ref> A 2011 randomized trial of mobile phone-based smoking cessation support in the UK found that a Txt2Stop cessation program significantly improved cessation rates at six months.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Free C, Knight R, Robertson S, Whittaker R, Edwards P, Zhou W, Rodgers A, Cairns J, Kenward MG, Roberts I | title = Smoking cessation support delivered via mobile phone text messaging (txt2stop): a single-blind, randomised trial | journal = Lancet | volume = 378 | issue = 9785 | pages = 49–55 | date = July 2011 | pmid = 21722952 | pmc = 3143315 | doi = 10.1016/s0140-6736(11)60701-0 }}</ref> A 2013 meta-analysis also noted "modest benefits" of mobile health interventions.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Free C, Phillips G, Watson L, Galli L, Felix L, Edwards P, Patel V, Haines A | title = The effectiveness of mobile-health technologies to improve health care service delivery processes: a systematic review and meta-analysis | journal = PLOS Medicine | volume = 10 | issue = 1 | article-number = e1001363 | date = 2013 | pmid = 23458994 | pmc = 3566926 | doi = 10.1371/journal.pmed.1001363 | doi-access = free }}</ref>
* Interactive web-based programs combined with a Mobile phone: Two RCTs documented long-term treatment effects (abstinence rate: 20-22%) of such interventions.<ref name="Brendryen">{{cite journal | vauthors = Brendryen H, Kraft P | title = Happy ending: a randomized controlled trial of a digital multi-media smoking cessation intervention | journal = Addiction | volume = 103 | issue = 3 | pages = 478–484; discussion 485–486 | date = March 2008 | pmid = 18269367 | doi = 10.1111/j.1360-0443.2007.02119.x | s2cid = 4638860 }}</ref><ref name="Brendryen, Drozd & Kraft">{{cite journal | vauthors = Brendryen H, Drozd F, Kraft P | title = A digital smoking cessation program delivered through internet and cell phone without nicotine replacement (happy ending): randomized controlled trial | journal = Journal of Medical Internet Research | volume = 10 | issue = 5 | pages = e51 | date = November 2008 | pmid = 19087949 | pmc = 2630841 | doi = 10.2196/jmir.1005 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

===Psychosocial approaches===
*The [[Great American Smokeout]] is an annual event that invites smokers to quit for one day, hoping they will be able to extend this forever.<ref>{{Cite web |title=History of the Great American Smokeout |url=http://www.cancer.org/healthy/stayawayfromtobacco/greatamericansmokeout/history-of-the-great-american-smokeout |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121019174015/http://www.cancer.org/healthy/stayawayfromtobacco/greatamericansmokeout/history-of-the-great-american-smokeout |archive-date=2012-10-19 |access-date=2026-01-24 |website=www.cancer.org |language=en}}</ref>
*The World Health Organization's [[World No Tobacco Day]] is held on May 31 each year.
*Smoking-cessation support is often offered over the telephone [[quitline]]s<ref name=Zhu2002>{{cite journal | vauthors = Zhu SH, Anderson CM, Tedeschi GJ, Rosbrook B, Johnson CE, Byrd M, Gutiérrez-Terrell E | title = Evidence of real-world effectiveness of a telephone quitline for smokers | journal = The New England Journal of Medicine | volume = 347 | issue = 14 | pages = 1087–1093 | date = October 2002 | pmid = 12362011 | doi = 10.1056/NEJMsa020660 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref name=Helgason2004>{{cite journal | vauthors = Helgason AR, Tomson T, Lund KE, Galanti R, Ahnve S, Gilljam H | title = Factors related to abstinence in a telephone helpline for smoking cessation | journal = European Journal of Public Health | volume = 14 | issue = 3 | pages = 306–310 | date = September 2004 | pmid = 15369039 | doi = 10.1093/eurpub/14.3.306 | doi-access = free }}</ref> (e.g., the US toll-free number 1-800-QUIT-NOW), or in person. Three meta-analyses have concluded that telephone cessation support is effective when compared with minimal or no counselling or self-help and that telephone cessation support with medication is more effective than medication alone,<ref name=USDHHS2008/>{{rp|91–92}}<ref name=Hopkins2001/>{{rp|40–42}} and that intensive individual counselling is more effective than the brief personal counselling intervention.<ref name="Individual behavioural counselling">{{cite journal | vauthors = Lancaster T, Stead LF | title = Individual behavioural counselling for smoking cessation | journal = The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | volume = 2018 | issue = 3 | article-number = CD001292 | date = March 2017 | pmid = 28361496 | pmc = 6464359 | doi = 10.1002/14651858.CD001292.pub3 }}</ref> A slight tendency towards better results for more intensive counselling was also observed in another meta-analysis. This analysis distinguished between reactive (smokers calling quitlines) and proactive (smokers receiving calls) interventions. For people who called the quitline themselves, additional calls helped to quit smoking for six months or longer. When proactively initiating contact with a smoker, telephone counselling increased the chances of smoking cessation by 2–4% compared with people who received no calls.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Matkin W, Ordóñez-Mena JM, Hartmann-Boyce J | title = Telephone counselling for smoking cessation | journal = The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | volume = 2019 | issue = 5 | article-number = CD002850 | date = May 2019 | pmid = 31045250 | pmc = 6496404 | doi = 10.1002/14651858.CD002850.pub4 | collaboration = Cochrane Tobacco Addiction Group }}</ref> There is about 10% to 25% increase in the chance of smoking cessation success with more behavioral support provided in person or via telephone when used as an adjunct to pharmacotherapy.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Hartmann-Boyce J, Hong B, Livingstone-Banks J, Wheat H, Fanshawe TR | title = Additional behavioural support as an adjunct to pharmacotherapy for smoking cessation | journal = The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | volume = 2019 | issue = 6 | article-number = CD009670 | date = June 2019 | pmid = 31166007 | pmc = 6549450 | doi = 10.1002/14651858.CD009670.pub4 }}</ref>
*Online social cessation networks attempt to emulate offline group cessation models using purpose built web applications. They are designed to promote [[online social support]] and encouragement for smokers when (usually automatically calculated) milestones are reached. Early studies have shown social cessation to be especially effective with smokers aged 19–29.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Baskerville NB, Azagba S, Norman C, McKeown K, Brown KS | title = Effect of a Digital Social Media Campaign on Young Adult Smoking Cessation | journal = Nicotine & Tobacco Research | volume = 18 | issue = 3 | pages = 351–360 | date = March 2016 | pmid = 26045252 | doi = 10.1093/ntr/ntv119 }}</ref>
*Group or individual psychological support can help people who want to quit. Recently, group therapy has been more helpful than self-help and some other individual intervention.<ref name="Group behaviour therapy programmes">{{cite journal | vauthors = Stead LF, Carroll AJ, Lancaster T | title = Group behaviour therapy programmes for smoking cessation | journal = The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | volume = 2017 | issue = 3 | article-number = CD001007 | date = March 2017 | pmid = 28361497 | pmc = 6464070 | doi = 10.1002/14651858.CD001007.pub3 }}</ref> The psychological support form of counselling can be effective alone; combining it with medication is more effective, and the number of support sessions with medication correlates with effectiveness.<ref name=USDHHS2008/>{{rp|89–90,101–103}}<ref name="Group behaviour therapy programmes"/><ref name="Individual behavioural counselling"/> The counselling styles that have been effective in smoking cessation activities include [[motivational interviewing]],<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Lindson-Hawley N, Thompson TP, Begh R | title = Motivational interviewing for smoking cessation | journal = The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | issue = 3 | article-number = CD006936 | date = March 2015 | pmid = 25726920 | doi = 10.1002/14651858.CD006936.pub3 | pmc = 6699669 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Hettema JE, Hendricks PS | title = Motivational interviewing for smoking cessation: a meta-analytic review | journal = Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology | volume = 78 | issue = 6 | pages = 868–884 | date = December 2010 | pmid = 21114344 | doi = 10.1037/a0021498 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Heckman CJ, Egleston BL, Hofmann MT | title = Efficacy of motivational interviewing for smoking cessation: a systematic review and meta-analysis | journal = Tobacco Control | volume = 19 | issue = 5 | pages = 410–416 | date = October 2010 | pmid = 20675688 | pmc = 2947553 | doi = 10.1136/tc.2009.033175 }}</ref> [[cognitive behavioral therapy]]<ref>{{cite book |vauthors=Perkins KA, Conklin CA, Levine MD |title= Cognitive-behavioral therapy for smoking cessation: a practical guidebook to the most effective treatment |year= 2008 |publisher= Routledge |location= New York |isbn= 978-0-415-95463-1}}</ref> and [[acceptance and commitment therapy]],<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors= Ruiz FJ |year=2010 |title=A review of Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) empirical evidence: Correlational, experimental psychopathology, component and outcome studies |journal=International Journal of Psychology and Psychological Therapy |volume=10 |issue=1 |pages=125–162 |url=https://www.ijpsy.com/volumen10/num1/256.html}}</ref> methods based on cognitive behavioral therapy.
*The Freedom From Smoking group clinic includes eight sessions and features a step-by-step plan for quitting smoking. Each session is designed to help smokers gain control over their behavior. The clinic format encourages participants to work on the process and problems of quitting both individually and as part of a group.<ref>{{cite web |title=About Freedom From Smoking|url=https://www.lung.org/stop-smoking/join-freedom-from-smoking/about-freedom-from-smoking.html|website=American Lung Association}}</ref>
*Multiple formats of psychosocial interventions increase quit rates: 10.8% for no intervention, 15.1% for one format, 18.5% for 2 formats, and 23.2% for three or four formats.<ref name=USDHHS2008/>{{rp|91}}
*The [[transtheoretical model]], including "stages of change", has been used in tailoring smoking cessation methods to individuals,<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Prochaska JO, Velicer WF, DiClemente CC, Fava J | title = Measuring processes of change: applications to the cessation of smoking | journal = Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology | volume = 56 | issue = 4 | pages = 520–528 | date = August 1988 | pmid = 3198809 | doi = 10.1037/0022-006X.56.4.520 | url = https://digitalcommons.uri.edu/psy_facpubs/553 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = DiClemente CC, Prochaska JO, Fairhurst SK, Velicer WF, Velasquez MM, Rossi JS | title = The process of smoking cessation: an analysis of precontemplation, contemplation, and preparation stages of change | journal = Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology | volume = 59 | issue = 2 | pages = 295–304 | date = April 1991 | pmid = 2030191 | doi = 10.1037/0022-006X.59.2.295 | url = http://www.uri.edu/research/cprc/Publications/PDFs/ByTitle/The%20Process%20of%20smoking%20cessation%20an%20analysis%20of%20precomtemplation.pdf | url-status = unfit | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20110606230703/http://www.uri.edu/research/cprc/Publications/PDFs/ByTitle/The%20Process%20of%20smoking%20cessation%20an%20analysis%20of%20precomtemplation.pdf | archive-date = 2011-06-06 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Velicer WF, Prochaska JO, Rossi JS, Snow MG | title = Assessing outcome in smoking cessation studies | journal = Psychological Bulletin | volume = 111 | issue = 1 | pages = 23–41 | date = January 1992 | pmid = 1539088 | doi = 10.1037/0033-2909.111.1.23 | url = https://digitalcommons.uri.edu/psy_facpubs/536 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Prochaska JO, DiClemente CC, Velicer WF, Rossi JS | title = Standardized, individualized, interactive, and personalized self-help programs for smoking cessation | journal = Health Psychology | volume = 12 | issue = 5 | pages = 399–405 | date = September 1993 | pmid = 8223364 | doi = 10.1037/0278-6133.12.5.399 | url = http://www.uri.edu/research/cprc/Publications/PDFs/ByTitle/Standardized%20individualized%20interactive%20and%20Personalized.pdf | url-status = unfit | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20110606231216/http://www.uri.edu/research/cprc/Publications/PDFs/ByTitle/Standardized%20individualized%20interactive%20and%20Personalized.pdf | archive-date = 2011-06-06 }}</ref> however, there is some evidence to suggest that "stage-based self-help interventions (expert systems and/or tailored materials) and individual counselling are neither more nor less effective than their non-stage-based equivalents."<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Cahill K, Lancaster T, Green N | title = Stage-based interventions for smoking cessation | journal = The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | issue = 11 | article-number = CD004492 | date = November 2010 | pmid = 21069681 | doi = 10.1002/14651858.CD004492.pub4 | veditors = Cahill K }}</ref>

==== How to set a quit date ====
Most smoking cessation resources such as the [[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]] (CDC)<ref name="CDC Web">{{cite web |title=Making a Quit Plan |url=https://www.cdc.gov/tobacco/campaign/tips/quit-smoking/guide/quit-plan.html |access-date=19 October 2015 |website=Centers for Disease Control and Prevention}}</ref> and [[Mayo Clinic|The Mayo Clinic]]<ref name="mayoclinic">{{cite web |title=Preparing for Quit Day |url=https://www.mayoclinic.org/healthy-lifestyle/quit-smoking/in-depth/smoking-cessation/art-20045441 |access-date=19 October 2015 |website=Mayo Clinic }}</ref> encourage smokers to create a quit plan, including setting a quit date, which helps them anticipate and plan for smoking challenges. A quit plan can improve a smoker's chance of a successful quit<ref name="SmitAB">{{cite journal | vauthors = Smit ES, Hoving C, Schelleman-Offermans K, West R, de Vries H | title = Predictors of successful and unsuccessful quit attempts among smokers motivated to quit | journal = Addictive Behaviors | volume = 39 | issue = 9 | pages = 1318–1324 | date = September 2014 | pmid = 24837754 | doi = 10.1016/j.addbeh.2014.04.017 | url = https://dare.uva.nl/personal/pure/en/publications/predictors-of-successful-and-unsuccessful-quit-attempts-among-smokers-motivated-to-quit(f1e3a649-0fc6-41c7-a382-55d223f3943a).html }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = de Vries H, Eggers SM, Bolman C | title = The role of action planning and plan enactment for smoking cessation | journal = BMC Public Health | volume = 13 | article-number = 393 | date = April 2013 | pmid = 23622256 | pmc = 3644281 | doi = 10.1186/1471-2458-13-393 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref name="bolmana">{{cite journal | vauthors = Bolman C, Eggers SM, van Osch L, Te Poel F, Candel M, de Vries H | title = Is Action Planning Helpful for Smoking Cessation? Assessing the Effects of Action Planning in a Web-Based Computer-Tailored Intervention | journal = Substance Use & Misuse | volume = 50 | issue = 10 | pages = 1249–1260 | date = Oct 2015 | pmid = 26440754 | doi = 10.3109/10826084.2014.977397 | s2cid = 20337590 | url = https://cris.maastrichtuniversity.nl/en/publications/d8f32243-608d-4abb-a015-19aba329421f }}</ref> as can setting Monday, as the quit date, given that research has shown that Monday more than any other day is when smokers are seeking information online to quit smoking<ref name="Ayers">{{cite journal | vauthors = Ayers JW, Althouse BM, Johnson M, Cohen JE | title = Circaseptan (weekly) rhythms in smoking cessation considerations | journal = JAMA Internal Medicine | volume = 174 | issue = 1 | pages = 146–148 | date = January 2014 | pmid = 24166181 | pmc = 4670616 | doi = 10.1001/jamainternmed.2013.11933 }}</ref> and calling state quitlines.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Erbas B, Bui Q, Huggins R, Harper T, White V | title = Investigating the relation between placement of Quit antismoking advertisements and number of telephone calls to Quitline: a semiparametric modelling approach | journal = Journal of Epidemiology and Community Health | volume = 60 | issue = 2 | pages = 180–182 | date = February 2006 | pmid = 16415271 | pmc = 2566152 | doi = 10.1136/jech.2005.038109 }}</ref> In Nepal, '''smokers are not selfish,''' a [[health campaign]] of two weeks is started on the occasion of [[Valentine's Day]] and [[Vasant Panchami]] to motivate individuals to quit smoking as a sacrifice for their loved ones and making it a meaningful decision of life. This campaign is taking public attention.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Dr Anil Om Murthi Archives |url=https://enewspolar.com/tag/dr-anil-om-murthi/ |access-date=2024-02-05 |website=Enewspolar |language=en}}</ref>

==== Self-help ====
[[File:Text messaging used to provide encouragement to quit smoking.png|thumb|right|Some health organizations manage text messaging services to help people avoid smoking.]]
Self-help materials may produce a small increase in quit rates specially when there is no other supporting intervention form.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Livingstone-Banks J, Ordóñez-Mena JM, Hartmann-Boyce J | title = Print-based self-help interventions for smoking cessation | journal = The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | volume = 1 | issue = 1 | article-number = CD001118 | date = January 2019 | pmid = 30623970 | pmc = 7112723 | doi = 10.1002/14651858.CD001118.pub4 }}</ref> "The effect of self-help was weak", and the number of types of self-help did not produce higher abstinence rates.<ref name=USDHHS2008/>{{rp|89–91}} Nevertheless, self-help modalities for smoking cessation include:
*In-person self-help groups such as [[Nicotine Anonymous]],<ref>{{cite web |title=Nicotine Anonymous offers help for those who desire to live free from nicotine |url=https://nicotine-anonymous.org/|website=nicotine-anonymous.org}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Glasser I | title = Nicotine anonymous may benefit nicotine-dependent individuals | journal = American Journal of Public Health | volume = 100 | issue = 2 | pages = 196; author reply 196-196; author reply 197 | date = February 2010 | pmid = 20019295 | pmc = 2804638 | doi = 10.2105/ajph.2009.181545 }}</ref> or web-based cessation resources such as [https://smokefree.gov/ Smokefree.gov], which offers various types of assistance including self-help materials.<ref>{{cite web |last1=U.S. Department of Health and Human Services|title=MySmokeFree: Your personalized quit experience |url=https://smokefree.gov/|website=Smokefree.gov}}</ref>
*WebMD: a resource providing health information, tools for managing health, and support.<ref>{{cite web |title=Slideshow: 13 Best Quit-Smoking Tips Ever|url=https://www.webmd.com/smoking-cessation/ss/slideshow-13-best-quit-smoking-tips-ever|website=WebMD}}</ref>
*[[Self-help|Self-help books]] such as [[Allen Carr]]'s ''Easy Way to Stop Smoking''.<ref name=Carr2004>{{cite book | vauthors=Carr A |title= The easy way to stop smoking |year= 2004 |publisher= Sterling |location= New York |isbn= 978-1-4027-7163-7}}</ref>
*[[Spirituality]]: In one survey of adult smokers, 88% reported a history of spiritual practice or belief, and of those more than three-quarters were of the opinion that using spiritual resources may help them quit smoking.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Gonzales D, Redtomahawk D, Pizacani B, Bjornson WG, Spradley J, Allen E, Lees P | title = Support for spirituality in smoking cessation: results of pilot survey | journal = Nicotine & Tobacco Research | volume = 9 | issue = 2 | pages = 299–303 | date = February 2007 | pmid = 17365761 | doi = 10.1080/14622200601078582 }}</ref>
*A review of [[mindfulness]] training as a treatment for addiction showed reduction in craving and smoking following training.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Tang YY, Tang R, Posner MI | title = Mindfulness meditation improves emotion regulation and reduces drug abuse | journal = Drug and Alcohol Dependence | volume = 163 Suppl 1 | issue = Suppl 1 | pages = S13–S18 | date = June 2016 | pmid = 27306725 | doi = 10.1016/j.drugalcdep.2015.11.041 | doi-access = free }}</ref>
*Physical activities help in the maintenance of smoking cessation even if there is no conclusive evidence of the most appropriate exercise intensity.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Ussher MH, Faulkner GE, Angus K, Hartmann-Boyce J, Taylor AH | title = Exercise interventions for smoking cessation | journal = The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | volume = 2019 | issue = 10 | date = October 2019 | pmid = 31684691 | pmc = 6819982 | doi = 10.1002/14651858.CD002295.pub6 }}</ref>

====Biochemical feedback====
Various methods allow a smoker to see the impact of their tobacco use and the immediate effects of quitting. Using biochemical feedback methods can allow tobacco users to be identified and assessed, and monitoring throughout an effort to quit can increase motivation to quit.<ref name="Bittoun">{{cite journal |vauthors= Bittoun R |year= 2008 |title= Carbon monoxide meter: The essential clinical tool- the 'stethoscope"-of smoking cessation |journal= Journal of Smoking Cessation |volume= 3 |issue= 2 |pages= 69–70 |doi=10.1375/jsc.3.2.69|doi-access= free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Jamrozik K, Vessey M, Fowler G, Wald N, Parker G, Van Vunakis H | title = Controlled trial of three different antismoking interventions in general practice | journal = British Medical Journal | volume = 288 | issue = 6429 | pages = 1499–1503 | date = May 1984 | pmid = 6426618 | pmc = 1441184 | doi = 10.1136/bmj.288.6429.1499 }}</ref> Evidence-wise, little is known about the effects of using biomechanical tests to determine a person's risk related to smoking cessation.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Clair C, Mueller Y, Livingstone-Banks J, Burnand B, Camain JY, Cornuz J, Rège-Walther M, Selby K, Bize R | title = Biomedical risk assessment as an aid for smoking cessation | journal = The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | volume = 2019 | issue = 3 | article-number = CD004705 | date = March 2019 | pmid = 30912847 | pmc = 6434771 | doi = 10.1002/14651858.CD004705.pub5 }}</ref>

*Breath carbon monoxide (CO) monitoring: [[carbon monoxide]] is a significant component of cigarette smoke, and a [[breath carbon monoxide monitor]] can be used to detect current cigarette use. Carbon monoxide concentration in breath is directly correlated with the CO concentration in blood, known as percent [[carboxyhemoglobin]]. The value of demonstrating blood CO concentration to a smoker through a non-invasive breath sample is that it links the smoking habit with the physiological harm associated with smoking.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Irving JM, Clark EC, Crombie IK, Smith WC | title = Evaluation of a portable measure of expired-air carbon monoxide | journal = Preventive Medicine | volume = 17 | issue = 1 | pages = 109–115 | date = January 1988 | pmid = 3362796 | doi = 10.1016/0091-7435(88)90076-x }}</ref> CO concentrations show a noticeable decrease within hours of quitting, which can encourage someone to work on quitting. Breath CO monitoring has been utilized in smoking cessation as a tool to provide patients with biomarker feedback, similar to how other diagnostic tools such as the stethoscope, the blood pressure cuff, and the cholesterol test have been used by treatment professionals in medicine.<ref name="Bittoun"/>
*Cotinine: [[Cotinine]], a [[metabolite]] of nicotine, is present in smokers. Like carbon monoxide, a cotinine test can be a reliable biomarker to determine smoking status.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Florescu A, Ferrence R, Einarson T, Selby P, Soldin O, Koren G | title = Methods for quantification of exposure to cigarette smoking and environmental tobacco smoke: focus on developmental toxicology | journal = Therapeutic Drug Monitoring | volume = 31 | issue = 1 | pages = 14–30 | date = February 2009 | pmid = 19125149 | pmc = 3644554 | doi = 10.1097/FTD.0b013e3181957a3b }}</ref> Cotinine levels can be tested through urine, saliva, blood, or hair samples. One of the main concerns of cotinine testing is the invasiveness of typical sampling methods.

While both measures offer high sensitivity and specificity, they differ in usage method and cost. For example, breath CO monitoring is non-invasive, while cotinine testing relies on bodily fluid. For instance, these two methods can be used alone or together when abstinence verification needs additional confirmation.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = McClure JB | title = Are biomarkers a useful aid in smoking cessation? A review and analysis of the literature | journal = Behavioral Medicine | volume = 27 | issue = 1 | pages = 37–47 | year = 2001 | pmid = 11575171 | doi = 10.1080/08964280109595770 | s2cid = 25616883 }}</ref>

====Competitions and incentives====
Financial or material incentives to entice people to quit smoking improve smoking cessation while the motivation is in place.<ref name=":6">{{cite journal | vauthors = Notley C, Gentry S, Livingstone-Banks J, Bauld L, Perera R, Conde M, Hartmann-Boyce J | title = Incentives for smoking cessation | journal = The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | volume = 1 | issue = 1 | article-number = CD004307 | date = January 2025 | pmid = 39799985 | pmc = 11725379 | doi = 10.1002/14651858.CD004307.pub7 }}</ref> Competitions that require participants to deposit their own money, "betting" that they will succeed in quitting smoking, appear to be an effective incentive.<ref name=":6" /> However, it is more difficult to recruit participants for this type of contest in head-to-head comparisons with other incentive models, such as giving participants [[Nicotine replacement therapy|NRT]] or placing them in a more typical rewards program.<ref name="SmokCessIncentives">{{cite journal | vauthors = Halpern SD, French B, Small DS, Saulsgiver K, Harhay MO, Audrain-McGovern J, Loewenstein G, Brennan TA, Asch DA, Volpp KG | title = Randomized trial of four financial-incentive programs for smoking cessation | journal = The New England Journal of Medicine | volume = 372 | issue = 22 | pages = 2108–2117 | date = May 2015 | pmid = 25970009 | pmc = 4471993 | doi = 10.1056/NEJMoa1414293 | author3-link = Dylan S. Small }}</ref> Evidence also shows that incentive programs are effective for pregnant mothers who smoke both during pregnancy and post-partum.<ref name=":6" /> As of 2019, there is an insufficient number of studies on "quit and win," and other competition-based interventions and results from the existing studies were inconclusive.<ref name="FanshaweHartmann-Boyce2019">{{cite journal | vauthors = Fanshawe TR, Hartmann-Boyce J, Perera R, Lindson N | title = Competitions for smoking cessation | journal = The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | volume = 2019 | issue = 2 | article-number = CD013272 | date = February 2019 | pmid = 30784046 | pmc = 6953205 | doi = 10.1002/14651858.CD013272 }}</ref>

In 2026, Colorado QuitLine started offering a $100 incentive for Coloradans completing a coaching program designed to help quit tobacco and nicotine products.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-03-04 |title=Colorado Quitline offers up $100 incentive for people to quit smoking |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/colorado/news/colorado-quitline-100-dollar-incentive-smoking-nicotine/ |access-date=2026-06-11 |website=www.cbsnews.com |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Colorado QuitLine offers up to $100 incentive to help adults across the state quit tobacco and nicotine products {{!}} Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment |url=https://cdphe.colorado.gov/press-release/colorado-quitline-offers-up-to-100-incentive-to-help-adults-across-the-state-quit |access-date=2026-06-11 |website=cdphe.colorado.gov}}</ref> The program itself claims a 35% success rate.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Kick Nicotine to the Curb with Personalized Support |url=https://www.coloradoquits.com/ |access-date=2026-06-11 |website=www.coloradoquits.com}}</ref>

===== Workplace incentives =====
A 2008 [[Cochrane Library|Cochrane]] review of smoking cessation activities in work-places concluded that "interventions directed towards individual smokers increase the likelihood of quitting smoking".<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Cahill K, Lancaster T | title = Workplace interventions for smoking cessation | journal = The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | volume = 2014 | issue = 2 | article-number = CD003440 | date = February 2014 | pmid = 24570145 | pmc = 11285308 | doi = 10.1002/14651858.CD003440.pub4 }}</ref> A 2010 systematic review determined that worksite incentives and competitions needed to be combined with additional interventions to produce significant increases in smoking cessation rates.<ref name="Leeks2010">{{cite journal | vauthors = Leeks KD, Hopkins DP, Soler RE, Aten A, Chattopadhyay SK | title = Worksite-based incentives and competitions to reduce tobacco use. A systematic review | journal = American Journal of Preventive Medicine | volume = 38 | issue = 2 Suppl | pages = S263–S274 | date = February 2010 | pmid = 20117611 | doi = 10.1016/j.amepre.2009.10.034 }}</ref>

===Healthcare systems===
Interventions delivered via healthcare providers and healthcare systems have been shown to improve smoking cessation among people who visit those services.
*A clinic screening system (e.g., computer prompts) to identify whether or not a person smokes doubled abstinence rates, from 3.1% to 6.4%.<ref name=USDHHS2008/>{{rp|78–79}} Similarly, the Task Force on Community Preventive Services determined that provider reminders alone or with provider education effectively promote smoking cessation.<ref name=Hopkins2001>{{cite journal | vauthors = Hopkins DP, Briss PA, Ricard CJ, Husten CG, Carande-Kulis VG, Fielding JE, Alao MO, McKenna JW, Sharp DJ, Harris JR, Woollery TA, Harris KW | title = Reviews of evidence regarding interventions to reduce tobacco use and exposure to environmental tobacco smoke | journal = American Journal of Preventive Medicine | volume = 20 | issue = 2 Suppl | pages = 16–66 | date = February 2001 | pmid = 11173215 | doi = 10.1016/S0749-3797(00)00297-X }}</ref>{{rp|33–38}}
*A 2008 Guideline meta-analysis estimated that physician advice to quit smoking led to a quit rate of 10.2%, as opposed to a quit rate of 7.9% among patients who did not receive physician advice to quit smoking.<ref name=USDHHS2008/>{{rp|82–83}} Even brief advice from physicians may have "a small effect on cessation rates",<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Stead LF, Buitrago D, Preciado N, Sanchez G, Hartmann-Boyce J, Lancaster T | title = Physician advice for smoking cessation | journal = The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | volume = 2013 | issue = 5 | article-number = CD000165 | date = May 2013 | pmid = 23728631 | pmc = 7064045 | doi = 10.1002/14651858.CD000165.pub4 }}</ref> and there is evidence that the physicians' probability of giving smoking cessation advice declines with the person who smokes age.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Maguire CP, Ryan J, Kelly A, O'Neill D, Coakley D, Walsh JB | title = Do patient age and medical condition influence medical advice to stop smoking? | journal = Age and Ageing | volume = 29 | issue = 3 | pages = 264–266 | date = May 2000 | pmid = 10855911 | doi = 10.1093/ageing/29.3.264 | doi-access = free }}</ref> There is evidence that only 81% of smokers age 50 or greater received advice on quitting from their physicians in the preceding year.<ref name="Ossip-Klein-2000">{{cite journal | vauthors = Ossip-Klein DJ, McIntosh S, Utman C, Burton K, Spada J, Guido J | title = Smokers ages 50+: who gets physician advice to quit? | journal = Preventive Medicine | volume = 31 | issue = 4 | pages = 364–369 | date = October 2000 | pmid = 11006061 | doi = 10.1006/pmed.2000.0721 | doi-access = free }}</ref>
*For one-to-one or person-to-person counselling sessions, the duration of each session, the total contact time, and the number of sessions all correlated with the effectiveness of smoking cessation. For example, "Higher intensity" interventions (>10 minutes) produced a quit rate of 22.1% as opposed to 10.9% for "no contact" over 300 minutes of contact time made a quit rate of 25.5% as opposed to 11.0% for "no minutes" and more than 8 sessions produced a quit rate of 24.7% as opposed to 12.4% for 0–1 sessions.<ref name=USDHHS2008/>{{rp|83–86}}
*Both physicians and non-physicians increased abstinence rates compared with self-help or no clinicians.<ref name=USDHHS2008/>{{rp|87–88}} For example, a Cochrane review of 58 studies found that nursing interventions increased the likelihood of quitting.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Rice VH, Heath L, Livingstone-Banks J, Hartmann-Boyce J | title = Nursing interventions for smoking cessation | journal = The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | volume = 2017 | issue = 12 | article-number = CD001188 | date = December 2017 | pmid = 29243221 | pmc = 6486227 | doi = 10.1002/14651858.CD001188.pub5 }}</ref> Another review found some positive effects when trained community pharmacists support patients in their smoking cessation trials.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Carson-Chahhoud KV, Livingstone-Banks J, Sharrad KJ, Kopsaftis Z, Brinn MP, To-A-Nan R, Bond CM | title = Community pharmacy personnel interventions for smoking cessation | journal = The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | volume = 2019 | issue = 10 | date = October 2019 | pmid = 31684695 | pmc = 6822095 | doi = 10.1002/14651858.CD003698.pub3 }}</ref>
*Dental professionals also provide a key component in increasing tobacco abstinence rates in the community through counseling patients on the effects of tobacco on oral health in conjunction with an oral exam.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Holliday R, Hong B, McColl E, Livingstone-Banks J, Preshaw PM | title = Interventions for tobacco cessation delivered by dental professionals | journal = The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | volume = 2021 | issue = 2 | article-number = CD005084 | date = February 2021 | pmid = 33605440 | pmc = 8095016 | doi = 10.1002/14651858.CD005084.pub4 }}</ref>
*According to the 2008 Guideline, based on two studies the training of clinicians in smoking cessation methods may increase abstinence rates;<ref name=USDHHS2008/>{{rp|130}} however, a Cochrane review found and measured that such training decreased smoking in patients.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Carson KV, Verbiest ME, Crone MR, Brinn MP, Esterman AJ, Assendelft WJ, Smith BJ | title = Training health professionals in smoking cessation | journal = The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | volume = 2012 | issue = 5 | article-number = CD000214 | date = May 2012 | pmid = 22592671 | pmc = 10088066 | doi = 10.1002/14651858.CD000214.pub2 | hdl-access = free | veditors = Carson KV | hdl = 2066/110023 }}</ref>{{Update inline|reason=Updated version https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/41676926|date = April 2026}}
*Reducing or eliminating the costs of cessation therapies for smokers increased quit rates in three meta-analyses.<ref name=USDHHS2008/>{{rp|139–140}}<ref name=Hopkins2001/>{{rp|38–40}}<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = van den Brand FA, Nagelhout GE, Reda AA, Winkens B, Evers SM, Kotz D, van Schayck OC | title = Healthcare financing systems for increasing the use of tobacco dependence treatment | journal = The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | volume = 2017 | issue = 9 | article-number = CD004305 | date = September 2017 | pmid = 28898403 | pmc = 6483741 | doi = 10.1002/14651858.CD004305.pub5 }}</ref>
*In one systematic review and meta-analysis, multi-component interventions increased quit rates in [[primary care]] settings.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Papadakis S, McDonald P, Mullen KA, Reid R, Skulsky K, Pipe A | title = Strategies to increase the delivery of smoking cessation treatments in primary care settings: a systematic review and meta-analysis | journal = Preventive Medicine | volume = 51 | issue = 3–4 | pages = 199–213 | year = 2010 | pmid = 20600264 | doi = 10.1016/j.ypmed.2010.06.007 }}</ref> "Multi-component" interventions were defined as those that combined two or more of the following strategies known as the "5 A's":<ref name=USDHHS2008/>{{rp|38–43}}
**Ask — Systematically identify all tobacco users at every visit
**Advise — Strongly urge all tobacco users to quit[[File:Breath CO Monitor.jpg|thumb|upright=.65|Breath CO monitor displaying carbon monoxide concentration of an exhaled breath sample (in ppm) with its corresponding percent concentration of carboxyhemoglobin]]
**Assess — Determine willingness to make a quit attempt
**Assist — Aid the patient in quitting (provide counselling-style support and medication)
**Arrange — Ensure follow-up contact

===Substitutes for cigarettes===
{{Main|Nicotine replacement therapy|Electronic cigarette#Smoking cessation}}

*[[Nicotine replacement therapy]] (NRT) is the general term for using products that contain nicotine but not tobacco to aid smoking cessation. These include nicotine lozenges, [[nicotine gum]] and inhalers, [[nicotine patch]]es, and electronic cigarettes. In a review of 136 NRT-related Cochrane Tobacco Addiction Group studies, substantial evidence supported NRT use in increasing the chances of successfully quitting smoking by 50 to 60% in comparison to placebo or a non-NRT control group.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Hartmann-Boyce J, Chepkin SC, Ye W, Bullen C, Lancaster T | title = Nicotine replacement therapy versus control for smoking cessation | journal = The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | volume = 5 | issue = 5 | article-number = CD000146 | date = May 2018 | pmid = 29852054 | pmc = 6353172 | doi = 10.1002/14651858.CD000146.pub5 | collaboration = Cochrane Tobacco Addiction Group }}</ref>
*[[Electronic cigarette|Electronic cigarettes (ECs)]]: There is high‐certainty evidence that ECs with nicotine increase quit rates compared to NRT and moderate‐certainty evidence that they increase quit rates compared to ECs without nicotine.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Hartmann-Boyce J, Lindson N, Butler AR, McRobbie H, Bullen C, Begh R, Theodoulou A, Notley C, Rigotti NA, Turner T, Fanshawe TR, Hajek P | title = Electronic cigarettes for smoking cessation | journal = The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | volume = 11 | issue = 11 | article-number = CD010216 | date = November 2022 | pmid = 36384212 | pmc = 9668543 | doi = 10.1002/14651858.CD010216.pub7 }}</ref>{{Update inline|reason=Updated version https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/38189560|date = February 2024}} Little is known regarding the long-term harms related to vaping.<ref name=FormanekSalisbury-Afshar2018>{{cite journal | vauthors = Formanek P, Salisbury-Afshar E, Afshar M | title = Helping Patients With ESRD and Earlier Stages of CKD to Quit Smoking | journal = American Journal of Kidney Diseases | volume = 72 | issue = 2 | pages = 255–266 | date = August 2018 | pmid = 29661542 | pmc = 6057817 | doi = 10.1053/j.ajkd.2018.01.057 }}</ref> A 2016 UK [[Royal College of Physicians]] report supports using e-cigarettes as a smoking cessation tool.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Royal College of Physicians|title=RCP statement on e-cigarettes |url=https://www.rcplondon.ac.uk/news/rcp-statement-e-cigarettes|website=RCP London|date=25 June 2014}}</ref> A 2015 [[Public Health England]] report stated that "Smokers who have tried other methods of quitting without success could be encouraged to try e-cigarettes (EC) to stop smoking and stop smoking services should support smokers using EC to quit by offering them behavioural support."<ref name=McNeill2015>{{cite web |vauthors= McNeill A, Brose LS, Calder R, Hitchman SC, Hajek P, McRobbie H |url= https://www.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/454516/Ecigarettes_an_evidence_update_A_report_commissioned_by_Public_Health_England.pdf |title=E-cigarettes: an evidence update|location=UK|publisher=Public Health England |page=6 |date=August 2015}}</ref> However, since little is known about long term effects, other regulated options such as nicotine replacement therapy, varenicline or bupropion should be discussed primarily.

===Alternative approaches===
[[File:PEZ PEZ.Die.süße.Freude Braun 5way DE.AT-01.png|thumb|150px|A [[Pez]] vending machine. Pez was invented in 1927 as a smoking cessation aid, serving as an alternative to tobacco.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The History of PEZ - About Us |url=https://us.pez.com/pages/history |access-date=2024-06-01 |website=PEZ Candy |language=en}}</ref>]]

Most of the alternative approaches below have minimal evidence to support their use, and their efficacy and safety should be discussed with a healthcare professional before starting. 
*[[Acupuncture]]: Acupuncture has been explored as an adjunct treatment method for smoking cessation.<ref name="He">{{cite journal | vauthors = He D, Berg JE, Høstmark AT | title = Effects of acupuncture on smoking cessation or reduction for motivated smokers | journal = Preventive Medicine | volume = 26 | issue = 2 | pages = 208–214 | date = March 1997 | pmid = 9085389 | doi = 10.1006/pmed.1996.0125 }}</ref> A 2014 Cochrane review was unable to make conclusions regarding acupuncture as the evidence is poor.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = White AR, Rampes H, Liu JP, Stead LF, Campbell J | title = Acupuncture and related interventions for smoking cessation | journal = The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | volume = 2014 | issue = 1 | article-number = CD000009 | date = January 2014 | pmid = 24459016 | pmc = 7263424 | doi = 10.1002/14651858.CD000009.pub4 }}</ref> A 2008 guideline found no difference between acupuncture and placebo, found no scientific studies supporting laser therapy based on acupuncture principles but without the needles.<ref name="USDHHS2008" />{{rp|99}}
*[[Hypnosis]]: Hypnosis often involves the hypnotherapist suggesting the unpleasant outcomes of smoking to the patient.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.webmd.com/smoking-cessation/hypnosis-for-quitting-smoking|title=Hypnosis for Quitting Smoking|publisher=WebMD|access-date=19 May 2012}}</ref> Clinical trials studying hypnosis and [[hypnotherapy]] as a method for smoking cessation have been inconclusive.<ref name="USDHHS2008" />{{rp|100}}<ref name="Barnes)2019" /><ref name="Johnson">{{cite journal | vauthors = Johnson DL, Karkut RT | title = Performance by gender in a stop-smoking program combining hypnosis and aversion | journal = Psychological Reports | volume = 75 | issue = 2 | pages = 851–857 | date = October 1994 | pmid = 7862796 | doi = 10.2466/pr0.1994.75.2.851 | s2cid = 39850409 }}</ref><ref name="Law">{{cite journal | vauthors = Law M, Tang JL | title = An analysis of the effectiveness of interventions intended to help people stop smoking | journal = Archives of Internal Medicine | volume = 155 | issue = 18 | pages = 1933–1941 | date = October 1995 | pmid = 7575046 | doi = 10.1001/archinte.1995.00430180025004 }}</ref> A Cochrane review was unable to find evidence of benefit of hypnosis in smoking cessation, and suggested if there is a beneficial effect, it is small at best.<ref name="Barnes)2019">{{cite journal | vauthors = Barnes J, McRobbie H, Dong CY, Walker N, Hartmann-Boyce J | title = Hypnotherapy for smoking cessation | journal = The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | volume = 2019 | issue = 6 | article-number = CD001008 | date = June 2019 | pmid = 31198991 | pmc = 6568235 | doi = 10.1002/14651858.CD001008.pub3 }}</ref> However, a randomized trial published in 2008 found that hypnosis and nicotine patches "compares favorably" with standard behavioral counseling and nicotine patches in 12-month quit rates.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Carmody TP, Duncan C, Simon JA, Solkowitz S, Huggins J, Lee S, Delucchi K | title = Hypnosis for smoking cessation: a randomized trial | journal = Nicotine & Tobacco Research | volume = 10 | issue = 5 | pages = 811–818 | date = May 2008 | pmid = 18569754 | doi = 10.1080/14622200802023833 | s2cid = 36395279 }}</ref>
*[[Herbal medicine]]: Many herbs have been studied as a method for smoking cessation, including [[lobelia]] and [[Hypericum perforatum|St John's wort]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Mayo Clinic|title=St. John's wort (Hypericum perforatum) Evidence |url=https://www.mayoclinic.org/drugs-supplements-st-johns-wort/art-20362212|website=Mayo Clinic}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Sood A, Ebbert JO, Prasad K, Croghan IT, Bauer B, Schroeder DR | title = A randomized clinical trial of St. John's wort for smoking cessation | journal = Journal of Alternative and Complementary Medicine | volume = 16 | issue = 7 | pages = 761–767 | date = July 2010 | pmid = 20590478 | pmc = 3110810 | doi = 10.1089/acm.2009.0445 }}</ref> The results are inconclusive, but St. Johns Wort shows few adverse events, but is a contraindication to many medications. Lobelia has been used to treat respiratory diseases like [[asthma]] and bronchitis, and has been used for smoking cessation because of chemical similarities to tobacco; lobelia is now listed in the [[Food and Drug Administration|FDA]]'s Poisonous Plant Database.<ref>{{cite web|last1=U.S. Food and Drug Administration|title=FDA Poisonous Plant Database|url=https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/plantox/|website=www.accessdata.fda.gov|access-date=2019-11-11|archive-date=2022-01-21|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220121131935/https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/Plantox/}}</ref> Lobelia can still be found in many products sold for smoking cessation and should be used with caution. Herbal products should be discussed with healthcare professionals before use to confirm safety with other medications.
*[[Smokeless tobacco]]: There is little smoking in Sweden, which is reflected in the very low cancer rates for Swedish men. Use of [[snus]] (a form of steam-pasteurized, rather than heat-pasteurized, air-cured smokeless tobacco) is an observed cessation method for Swedish men and even recommended by some Swedish doctors.<ref>{{cite report |author= Scientific Committee on Emerging and Newly Identified Health Risks (SCENIHR) |title= Health Effects of Smokeless Tobacco Products |page= 103 |url= http://ec.europa.eu/health/ph_risk/committees/04_scenihr/docs/scenihr_o_009.pdf}}</ref> However, the report by the [[Scientific Committee on Emerging and Newly Identified Health Risks]] (SCENIHR) concludes "STP (smokeless tobacco products) are addictive and their use is hazardous to health. Evidence on the effectiveness of STP as a smoking cessation aid is insufficient."<ref>{{cite web |last1=Scientific Committee on Emerging and Newly Identified Health Risks (SCENIHR)|title=Health effects of smokeless tobacco products|url=http://ec.europa.eu/health/ph_risk/committees/04_scenihr/docs/scenihr_o_013.pdf}}</ref> A recent national study on the use of alternative tobacco products, including snus, did not show that these products promote cessation.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Popova L, Ling PM | title = Alternative tobacco product use and smoking cessation: a national study | journal = American Journal of Public Health | volume = 103 | issue = 5 | pages = 923–930 | date = May 2013 | pmid = 23488521 | pmc = 3661190 | doi = 10.2105/ajph.2012.301070 }}</ref>
*[[Aversion therapy]] is a method of treatment which works by pairing the pleasurable stimulus of smoking with other unpleasant stimuli, for example in the form of a wearable wristband which administers an electric stimulus.<ref>{{Cite journal |title=Aversive Therapy For Smoking Cessation: Worth Revisiting? A feasibility Trial |url=https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article-abstract/146/1_MeetingAbstract/480/4461/Aversive-Therapy-For-Smoking-Cessation-Worth |access-date=2026-02-20 |journal=Pediatrics |date=2020 |volume=146 |pages=480–481 |doi=10.1542/peds.146.1MA5.480b | vauthors = Lee CR, Harrington K, Rochford L, Shah N, Pruitt C, Grant M |url-access=subscription }}</ref> A Cochrane review reported that there is insufficient evidence of its efficacy.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Hajek P, Stead LF | title = Aversive smoking for smoking cessation | journal = The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | volume = 2001 | issue = 3 | article-number = CD000546 | date = 2004 | pmid = 15266433 | pmc = 7045729 | doi = 10.1002/14651858.CD000546.pub2 }}</ref>
*[[Nicotine vaccine]]s: Nicotine vaccines (e.g., [[NicVAX]] and [[TA-NIC]]) work by reducing the amount of nicotine reaching the brain; however, this method of therapy needs more investigations to establish its role and determine its side effects.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Hartmann-Boyce J, Cahill K, Hatsukami D, Cornuz J | title = Nicotine vaccines for smoking cessation | journal = The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | volume = 2012 | issue = 8 | article-number = CD007072 | date = August 2012 | pmid = 22895958 | pmc = 6486305 | doi = 10.1002/14651858.CD007072.pub2 }}</ref>
*Technology and machine learning: Research studies using machine learning or [[artificial intelligence]] tools to provide feedback and communication with those who are trying to quit smoking are increasing, yet the findings are so far inconclusive.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Coughlin LN, Tegge AN, Sheffer CE, Bickel WK | title = A Machine-Learning Approach to Predicting Smoking Cessation Treatment Outcomes | journal = Nicotine & Tobacco Research | volume = 22 | issue = 3 | pages = 415–422 | date = March 2020 | pmid = 30508122 | pmc = 7297111 | doi = 10.1093/ntr/nty259 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Sadasivam RS, Borglund EM, Adams R, Marlin BM, Houston TK | title = Impact of a Collective Intelligence Tailored Messaging System on Smoking Cessation: The Perspect Randomized Experiment | journal = Journal of Medical Internet Research | volume = 18 | issue = 11 | pages = e285 | date = November 2016 | pmid = 27826134 | pmc = 5120237 | doi = 10.2196/jmir.6465 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Patrick H, Fujii CA, Glaser DB, Utley DS, Marler JD | title = A Comprehensive Digital Program for Smoking Cessation: Assessing Feasibility in a Single-Group Cohort Study | journal = JMIR mHealth and uHealth | volume = 6 | issue = 12 | article-number = e11708 | date = December 2018 | pmid = 30563807 | pmc = 6315234 | doi = 10.2196/11708 | doi-access = free }}</ref> A 2025 study examining the efficacy of real-time intervention using a smartband found it helpful for reducing smoking.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bold |first1=Krysten W. |last2=Mestre |first2=Luis M. |last3=Garrison |first3=Kathleen A. |last4=Gueorguieva |first4=Ralitza |last5=O'Malley |first5=Stephanie S. |last6=Fucito |first6=Lisa M. |date=2025-11-10 |title=Feasibility and efficacy of a real-time smoking intervention using wearable technology |journal=PLOS Digital Health |volume=4 |issue=11 |article-number=e0001086 |doi=10.1371/journal.pdig.0001086  |doi-access=free|issn=2767-3170 |pmc=12599971 |pmid=41212887}}</ref>
*[[Psilocybin]] has been being investigated as a potential smoking cessation aid for several years. In 2021, [[Johns Hopkins School of Medicine|Johns Hopkins Medicine]] was awarded a grant from the National Institutes of Health to explore the potential impacts of psilocybin and talk therapy on tobacco addiction.<ref>{{Cite web| vauthors=Marisol M |date=2021-10-20|title=Johns Hopkins receives first federal grant for psychedelic treatment research in 50 years|website=The Hub|language=en |url=https://hub.jhu.edu/2021/10/20/first-nih-grant-for-psychedelics-in-50-years/|access-date=2022-01-29}}</ref>

== Special populations ==

===Children and adolescents===
Methods used with children and adolescents include:
*Motivational enhancement<ref name="Fanshawe-2017">{{cite journal | vauthors = Fanshawe TR, Halliwell W, Lindson N, Aveyard P, Livingstone-Banks J, Hartmann-Boyce J | title = Tobacco cessation interventions for young people | journal = The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | volume = 2017 | issue = 11 | article-number = CD003289 | date = November 2017 | pmid = 29148565 | pmc = 6486118 | doi = 10.1002/14651858.CD003289.pub6 }}</ref>
*Psychological support<ref name="Fanshawe-2017"/>
*Youth anti-tobacco activities, including participation in sports
*School-based curricula, like [[life skills|life-skills]] training
*[[School nursing|School-based nurse]] counseling sessions<ref>{{cite web |vauthors= Phert L |title=Intensive Counseling of Students by School Nurses Does Not Have Larger Impact on Long-Term Smoking Rates Than Briefer Sessions {{!}} AHRQ Health Care Innovations Exchange |url=https://innovations.ahrq.gov/profiles/intensive-counseling-students-school-nurses-does-not-have-larger-impact-long-term-smoking|website=innovations.ahrq.gov |access-date=19 July 2016}}</ref>
*Access reduction to tobacco
*Anti-tobacco media<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Davis KC, Farrelly MC, Messeri P, Duke J | title = The impact of national smoking prevention campaigns on tobacco-related beliefs, intentions to smoke and smoking initiation: results from a longitudinal survey of youth in the United States | journal = International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health | volume = 6 | issue = 2 | pages = 722–740 | date = February 2009 | pmid = 19440412 | pmc = 2672353 | doi = 10.3390/ijerph6020722 | doi-access = free | bibcode = 2009IJERP...6..722D }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Allen JA, Duke JC, Davis KC, Kim AE, Nonnemaker JM, Farrelly MC | title = Using mass media campaigns to reduce youth tobacco use: a review | journal = American Journal of Health Promotion | volume = 30 | issue = 2 | pages = e71–e82 | date = Nov–Dec 2015 | pmid = 25372236 | doi = 10.4278/ajhp.130510-lit-237 | s2cid = 9297116 }}</ref>
*Family communication
Cochrane reviews, mainly of studies combining motivational enhancement and psychological support, concluded that "complex approaches" for smoking cessation among young people show promise.<ref name="Fanshawe-2017"/><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Carson KV, Brinn MP, Labiszewski NA, Esterman AJ, Chang AB, Smith BJ | title = Community interventions for preventing smoking in young people | journal = The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | volume = 2011 | issue = 7 | article-number = CD001291 | date = July 2011 | pmid = 21735383 | pmc = 11384554 | doi = 10.1002/14651858.CD001291.pub2 }}</ref> The 2008 US Guideline recommends counselling-style support for adolescent smokers on the basis of a meta-analysis of seven studies.<ref name=USDHHS2008/>{{rp|159–161}} Neither the Cochrane review nor the 2008 Guideline recommend medications for adolescents who smoke.

===Pregnant women===
[[Smoking and pregnancy|Smoking during pregnancy]] can cause adverse health effects in both the woman and the fetus. The 2008 US Guideline determined that "person-to-person psychosocial interventions" (typically including "intensive counseling") increased abstinence rates in pregnant women who smoke to 13.3%, compared with 7.6% in usual care.<ref name=USDHHS2008/>{{rp|165–167}} Mothers who smoke during pregnancy have a greater tendency towards [[Preterm birth|premature births]]. Their babies are often underdeveloped, have smaller organs, and weigh much less than the average baby weight. In addition, these babies have weaker immune systems, making them more susceptible to many diseases such as middle ear inflammations and asthmatic bronchitis, as well as metabolic conditions such as diabetes and hypertension, all of which can bring significant morbidity.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Mund M, Louwen F, Klingelhoefer D, Gerber A | title = Smoking and pregnancy--a review on the first major environmental risk factor of the unborn | journal = International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health | volume = 10 | issue = 12 | pages = 6485–6499 | date = November 2013 | pmid = 24351784 | pmc = 3881126 | doi = 10.3390/ijerph10126485 | doi-access = free | bibcode = 2013IJERP..10.6485M }}</ref> Additionally, a study published by [[American Academy of Pediatrics]] shows that smoking during pregnancy increases the chance of [[SIDS|sudden unexpected infant death]] ((SUID) or (SIDS)).<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Anderson TM, Lavista Ferres JM, Ren SY, Moon RY, Goldstein RD, Ramirez JM, Mitchell EA | title = Maternal Smoking Before and During Pregnancy and the Risk of Sudden Unexpected Infant Death | journal = Pediatrics | volume = 143 | issue = 4 | article-number = e20183325 | date = April 2019 | pmid = 30858347 | pmc = 6564075 | doi = 10.1542/peds.2018-3325 }}</ref> There is also an increased chance that the child will be a smoker in adulthood. A systematic review showed that psychosocial interventions help women quit smoking in late pregnancy and can reduce the incidence of low birth weight infants.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Chamberlain C, O'Mara-Eves A, Porter J, Coleman T, Perlen SM, Thomas J, McKenzie JE | title = Psychosocial interventions for supporting women to stop smoking in pregnancy | journal = The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | volume = 2 | issue = 2 | article-number = CD001055 | date = February 2017 | pmid = 28196405 | pmc = 4022453 | doi = 10.1002/14651858.CD001055.pub5 }}</ref>

It is a myth that a female smoker can cause harm to a fetus by quitting immediately upon discovering she is pregnant. This idea is not based on any medical study or fact.<ref>{{cite web |vauthors= Bowen M |title=Pregnancy and smoking|url=https://www.netdoctor.co.uk/conditions/pregnancy-and-family/a9099/pregnancy-and-smoking/|website=Netdoctor|access-date=19 July 2016|date=25 February 2013}}</ref>

In a UK study that included 1140 pregnant women, e-cigarettes were found to be as effective as nicotine patches at helping pregnant women to quit smoking. The safety of the two products was also similar.<ref>{{Cite journal |date=2022-11-04 |title=E-cigarettes may be better than nicotine patches in helping pregnant women stop smoking |url=https://evidence.nihr.ac.uk/alert/e-cigarettes-better-than-nicotine-patches-helping-pregnant-women-stop-smoking/ |journal=NIHR Evidence |language=en |doi=10.3310/nihrevidence_54425|s2cid=253360129 |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Hajek P, Przulj D, Pesola F, Griffiths C, Walton R, McRobbie H, Coleman T, Lewis S, Whitemore R, Clark M, Ussher M, Sinclair L, Seager E, Cooper S, Bauld L, Naughton F, Sasieni P, Manyonda I, Myers Smith K | title = Electronic cigarettes versus nicotine patches for smoking cessation in pregnancy: a randomized controlled trial | journal = Nature Medicine | volume = 28 | issue = 5 | pages = 958–964 | date = May 2022 | pmid = 35577966 | pmc = 9117131 | doi = 10.1038/s41591-022-01808-0 }}</ref> However, life style modification are the preferred method for pregnant women, and they should discuss smoking cessation techniques with a healthcare professional.

===Schizophrenia===
{{Main|Schizophrenia and tobacco smoking}}
Studies across 20 countries show a strong association between patients with schizophrenia and smoking. People with schizophrenia are much more likely to smoke than those without the disease.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = de Leon J, Diaz FJ | title = A meta-analysis of worldwide studies demonstrates an association between schizophrenia and tobacco smoking behaviors | journal = Schizophrenia Research | volume = 76 | issue = 2–3 | pages = 135–157 | date = July 2005 | pmid = 15949648 | doi = 10.1016/j.schres.2005.02.010 | s2cid = 32975940 }}</ref> For example, in the United States, 80% or more of people with schizophrenia smoke, compared to 20% of the general population in 2006.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Keltner NL, Grant JS | title = Smoke, smoke, smoke that cigarette | journal = Perspectives in Psychiatric Care | volume = 42 | issue = 4 | pages = 256–261 | date = November 2006 | pmid = 17107571 | doi = 10.1111/j.1744-6163.2006.00085.x }}</ref>

===Hospitalized smokers===
[[File:Smoking cessation-West&Shiffman.png|thumb|alt=Simple bar chart says "Varenicline + support" about 16, "NRT/bupropion + support" about 12.5, "NRT alone" about 7, "Telephone support" about 6, "Group support" about 5, "One-to-one support" about 4 and "Tailored online support" about 2.5.|Percent increase of success for six months over unaided attempts for each type of quitting (chart from West & Shiffman based on Cochrane review data<ref name=WestShiffman2007>{{cite book |vauthors=West R, Shiffman S |title=Fast facts: smoking cessation |publisher=Health Press Ltd|location=Abingdon, England |year=2007|edition=2nd|isbn=978-1-903734-98-8}}</ref>{{rp|59}})]]
Smokers who are hospitalised may be particularly motivated to quit.<ref name=USDHHS2008/>{{rp|149–150}} A 2012 Cochrane review found that interventions beginning during a hospital stay and continuing for one month or more after discharge were effective in producing abstinence.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Streck JM, Rigotti NA, Livingstone-Banks J, Tindle HA, Clair C, Munafò MR, Sterling-Maisel C, Hartmann-Boyce J | title = Interventions for smoking cessation in hospitalised patients | journal = The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | volume = 2024 | issue = 5 | article-number = CD001837 | date = May 2024 | pmid = 38770804 | pmc = 11106804 | doi = 10.1002/14651858.CD001837.pub4 }}</ref>

Patients undergoing elective surgery may get benefits of preoperative smoking cessation interventions, when starting 4–8 weeks before surgery with weekly counseling for behavioral support and use of [[nicotine replacement therapy]].<ref name="preop.">{{cite journal | vauthors = Thomsen T, Villebro N, Møller AM | title = Interventions for preoperative smoking cessation | journal = The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | volume = 2014 | issue = 3 | article-number = CD002294 | date = March 2014 | pmid = 24671929 | pmc = 7138216 | doi = 10.1002/14651858.CD002294.pub4 }}</ref> It is found to reduce the complications and the number of postoperative morbidity.<ref name="preop."/>

===Mood disorders===

People with [[mood disorder]]s or [[attention deficit hyperactivity disorder]]s have a greater chance to begin smoking and a lower chance of quitting smoking.<ref name="Moylan-2013" /> A higher correlation with smoking has also been seen in people diagnosed with the [[major depressive disorder]] at any time throughout their lifetime compared to those without it. Success rates in quitting smoking were lower for those with a major depressive disorder diagnosis versus people without the diagnosis.<ref name="Baggett-2013" /> Exposure to cigarette smoke early on in life, during pregnancy, infancy, or adolescence, may negatively impact a child's neurodevelopment and increase the risk of developing [[anxiety disorder]]s in the future.<ref name="Moylan-2013">{{cite journal | vauthors = Moylan S, Jacka FN, Pasco JA, Berk M | title = How cigarette smoking may increase the risk of anxiety symptoms and anxiety disorders: a critical review of biological pathways | journal = Brain and Behavior | volume = 3 | issue = 3 | pages = 302–326 | date = May 2013 | pmid = 23785661 | pmc = 3683289 | doi = 10.1002/brb3.137 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

===Homeless and poverty===
Homelessness doubles the likelihood of an individual currently being a smoker. Homelessness is independent of other socioeconomic factors and behavioral health conditions. Homeless individuals have the same rates of desire to quit smoking. Still, they are less likely than the general population to attempt to stop successfully.<ref name="Baggett-2013">{{cite journal | vauthors = Baggett TP, Lebrun-Harris LA, Rigotti NA | title = Homelessness, cigarette smoking and desire to quit: results from a US national study | journal = Addiction | volume = 108 | issue = 11 | pages = 2009–2018 | date = November 2013 | pmid = 23834157 | pmc = 3797258 | doi = 10.1111/add.12292 }}</ref><ref name="smokingcessationleadership.ucsf.edu-2015">{{cite web |url=https://smokingcessationleadership.ucsf.edu/other-vulnerable-populations|title=Other Vulnerable Populations |website=Smoking Cessation Leadership Center|date=8 September 2015|access-date=2017-06-29}}</ref>

In the United States, 60–80% of homeless adults are smokers. This is a considerably higher rate than the general adult population of 19%.<ref name="Baggett-2013"/> Many current smokers who are homeless report smoking as a means of coping with "all the pressure of being homeless."<ref name="Baggett-2013"/> The perception that homeless people smoking being "socially acceptable" can reinforce these trends.<ref name="Baggett-2013"/>

Americans under the poverty line have higher rates of smoking and lower rates of quitting than those over the poverty line.<ref name="smokingcessationleadership.ucsf.edu-2015"/><ref name="www.nationalhomeless.org">{{cite web |url=http://www.nationalhomeless.org/factsheets/tobacco.html|title=National Coalition for the Homeless|website=www.nationalhomeless.org|access-date=2017-06-29}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.cdc.gov/tobacco/data_statistics/fact_sheets/adult_data/cig_smoking/|title=CDC – Fact Sheet – Adult Cigarette Smoking in the United States – Smoking & Tobacco Use |author= CDC's Office on Smoking and Health |website=Smoking and Tobacco Use|language=en-us|access-date=2017-06-29}}</ref> While the homeless population is concerned about short-term effects of smoking, such as shortness of breath or recurrent bronchitis, they are not as concerned with long-term consequences.<ref name="www.nationalhomeless.org"/> The homeless population has unique barriers to quitting smoking, such as unstructured days, the stress of finding a job, and immediate survival needs that supersede the desire to quit smoking.<ref name="www.nationalhomeless.org"/>

These unique barriers can be combated through pharmacotherapy and behavioral counseling for high levels of nicotine dependence. The emphasis of immediate financial benefits to those who concern themselves with the short-term over the long-term, partnering with shelters to reduce the social acceptability of smoking in this population, and increased taxes on cigarettes and alternative tobacco products to further make the addiction more difficult to fund.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Baggett TP, Tobey ML, Rigotti NA | title = Tobacco use among homeless people--addressing the neglected addiction | journal = The New England Journal of Medicine | volume = 369 | issue = 3 | pages = 201–204 | date = July 2013 | pmid = 23863048 | doi = 10.1056/NEJMp1301935 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

=== Concurrent substance use disorders ===
Over three-quarters of people in treatment or recovery from substance misuse issues are current smokers.<ref name=":5">{{cite journal | vauthors = Iyahen EO, Omoruyi OO, Rowa-Dewar N, Dobbie F | title = Exploring the barriers and facilitators to the uptake of smoking cessation services for people in treatment or recovery from problematic drug or alcohol use: A qualitative systematic review | journal = PLOS ONE | volume = 18 | issue = 7 | article-number = e0288409 | date = 2023-07-13 | pmid = 37440505 | pmc = 10343091 | doi = 10.1371/journal.pone.0288409 | doi-access = free | bibcode = 2023PLoSO..1888409I }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Campbell BK, Le T, Andrews KB, Pramod S, Guydish J | title = Smoking among patients in substance use disorders treatment: associations with tobacco advertising, anti-tobacco messages, and perceived health risks | journal = The American Journal of Drug and Alcohol Abuse | volume = 42 | issue = 6 | pages = 649–656 | date = November 2016 | pmid = 27314450 | pmc = 5093078 | doi = 10.1080/00952990.2016.1183021 }}</ref> Providing behavioural interventions (such as counseling and advice) and pharmacotherapy including nicotine replacement therapy (such as the use of patches or gum, varenicline, and/or bupropion) increase tobacco abstinence that is sustainable and also reduces the risk of returning to other substance use.<ref name=":5" /><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Hartmann-Boyce J, Livingstone-Banks J, Ordóñez-Mena JM, Fanshawe TR, Lindson N, Freeman SC, Sutton AJ, Theodoulou A, Aveyard P | title = Behavioural interventions for smoking cessation: an overview and network meta-analysis | journal = The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | volume = 1 | issue = 1 | article-number = CD013229 | date = January 2021 | pmid = 33411338 | pmc = 11354481 | doi = 10.1002/14651858.CD013229.pub2 | s2cid = 230814023 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Apollonio D, Philipps R, Bero L | title = Interventions for tobacco use cessation in people in treatment for or recovery from substance use disorders | journal = The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | volume = 11 | issue = 11 | article-number = CD010274 | date = November 2016 | pmid = 27878808 | pmc = 6464324 | doi = 10.1002/14651858.CD010274.pub2 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Prochaska JJ, Delucchi K, Hall SM | title = A meta-analysis of smoking cessation interventions with individuals in substance abuse treatment or recovery | journal = Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology | volume = 72 | issue = 6 | pages = 1144–1156 | date = December 2004 | pmid = 15612860 | doi = 10.1037/0022-006X.72.6.1144 | url = https://www.escholarship.org/uc/item/0r8673wv }}</ref>

==Comparison of success rates==
Comparison of  success rates across interventions can be difficult because of different definitions of "success" used by the different studies.<ref name="ReferenceB">{{cite journal | vauthors = Rigotti NA, Clair C, Munafò MR, Stead LF | title = Interventions for smoking cessation in hospitalised patients | journal = The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | volume = 5 | issue = 5 | article-number = CD001837 | date = May 2012 | pmid = 22592676 | pmc = 4498489 | doi = 10.1002/14651858.CD001837.pub3 }}</ref>{{Update inline|reason=Updated version https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/38770804|date = March 2025}} Robert West and Saul Shiffman, authorities in this field recognized by government health departments in a number of countries,<ref name=WestShiffman2007/>{{rp|73,76,80}} have concluded that, used together, "behavioral support" and "medication" can quadruple the chances that a quit attempt will be successful.

A 2008 systematic review in the ''[[European Journal of Cancer Prevention]]'' found that group behavioural therapy was the most effective intervention strategy for smoking cessation, followed by [[bupropion]], intensive physician advice, nicotine replacement therapy, individual counselling, telephone counselling, nursing interventions, and tailored self-help interventions; the study did not discuss [[varenicline]].<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Lemmens V, Oenema A, Knut IK, Brug J | title = Effectiveness of smoking cessation interventions among adults: a systematic review of reviews | journal = European Journal of Cancer Prevention | volume = 17 | issue = 6 | pages = 535–544 | date = November 2008 | pmid = 18941375 | doi = 10.1097/cej.0b013e3282f75e48 | s2cid = 46131720 }}</ref>

==Factors affecting success==
[[File:Smoking insula.jpg|thumb|Individuals who sustained damage to the [[Insular cortex|insula]] were able to more easily abstain from smoking.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Naqvi NH, Rudrauf D, Damasio H, Bechara A | title = Damage to the insula disrupts addiction to cigarette smoking | journal = Science | volume = 315 | issue = 5811 | pages = 531–534 | date = January 2007 | pmid = 17255515 | pmc = 3698854 | doi = 10.1126/science.1135926 | bibcode = 2007Sci...315..531N }}</ref>]]There is an important social component to smoking. The spread of smoking cessation from person to person contributes to the decrease in smoking among different populations or groups.<ref name=autogenerated1>{{cite journal | vauthors = Christakis NA, Fowler JH | title = The collective dynamics of smoking in a large social network | journal = The New England Journal of Medicine | volume = 358 | issue = 21 | pages = 2249–2258 | date = May 2008 | pmid = 18499567 | pmc = 2822344 | doi = 10.1056/NEJMsa0706154 }}</ref> A 2008 study of a densely interconnected network of over 12,000 individuals found that smoking cessation by any given individual reduced the chances of others around them lighting up by the following amounts: a spouse by 67%, a sibling by 25%, a friend by 36%, and a coworker by 34%.<ref name=autogenerated1 /><!--For preceding ref, pmc deleted because PubMed Central version is author manuscript, not final.--> Nevertheless, a [[Cochrane (organization)|Cochrane]] review determined that interventions to increase social support for a smoker's cessation attempt did not improve long-term quit rates.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Faseru B, Richter KP, Scheuermann TS, Park EW | title = Enhancing partner support to improve smoking cessation | journal = The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | volume = 8 | issue = 8 | article-number = CD002928 | date = August 2018 | pmid = 30101972 | pmc = 6326744 | doi = 10.1002/14651858.CD002928.pub4 }}</ref>

Smokers trying to quit are faced with social influences that may persuade them to conform and continue smoking. Cravings are easier to detain when one's environment does not provoke the habit. Suppose a person who stopped smoking has close relationships with active smokers. In that case, they are often put into situations that make the urge to conform more tempting. However, in a small group with at least one other not smoking, the likelihood of conformity decreases. The social influence of smoking cigarettes has been proven to rely on simple variables. One researched variable depends on whether there is influence from a friend or non-friend.<ref name="Hitchman-2014" /> The research shows that individuals are 77% more likely to conform to non-friends, while close friendships decrease conformity. Therefore, if an acquaintance offers a cigarette as a polite gesture, the person who has stopped smoking will be likelier to break his commitment than if a friend had suggested it. Recent research from the International Tobacco Control (ITC) Four Country Survey of over 6,000 smokers found that smokers with fewer smoking friends were more likely to intend to quit and to succeed in their quit attempt.<ref name="Hitchman-2014">{{cite journal | vauthors = Hitchman SC, Fong GT, Zanna MP, Thrasher JF, Laux FL | title = The relation between number of smoking friends, and quit intentions, attempts, and success: findings from the International Tobacco Control (ITC) Four Country Survey | journal = Psychology of Addictive Behaviors | volume = 28 | issue = 4 | pages = 1144–1152 | date = December 2014 | pmid = 24841185 | pmc = 4266625 | doi = 10.1037/a0036483 }}</ref>

Expectations and attitude are significant factors. A self-perpetuating cycle occurs when a person feels bad for smoking yet smokes to alleviate feeling bad. Breaking that cycle can be a key in changing the sabotaging attitude.<ref>{{cite web|last1=American Cancer Society|title=Guide to Quitting Smoking|website=www.cancer.org|url=http://www.cancer.org/healthy/stayawayfromtobacco/guidetoquittingsmoking/|access-date=6 July 2016|archive-date=8 August 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160808163637/http://www.cancer.org/healthy/stayawayfromtobacco/guidetoquittingsmoking/}}</ref>
